entry.title: THE CAST-OFF OF APRIL STARTS THE CLINCHER OF SEPTEMBER — A SEVENTH EAST FLAG IN NINE YEARS IS SEWN ON AT HOUSTON: BRAVES 4, ASTROS 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 75 · Monday, the One-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE CAST-OFF OF APRIL STARTS THE CLINCHER OF SEPTEMBER — A SEVENTH EAST FLAG IN NINE YEARS IS SEWN ON AT HOUSTON: BRAVES 4, ASTROS 2

Pérez, judged surplus in the spring, keeps the ledger close; Yastrzemski's three-run thunder in the sixth — his third blow of the road trip — overturns Altuve's early lead; Mederos takes the decision, Dodd the save, and the sweep is complete; Houston, beaten a third straight time, sits a game off the West's throne with the wild-card ground shrinking beneath it

On the twelfth of April the Atlanta club looked upon Martín Pérez — a non-roster man of the spring — and designated him for assignment, which is the game's politest way of saying not wanted. On Sunday afternoon at Houston the same Pérez took the ball in the game that decided the National League's East, and kept it close enough for the deciding to be done. The manager Weiss has reminded his men all summer that the prognosticators wanted no part of them in March; it was fitting, then, that the flag was clinched behind a pitcher the ledger itself had once declined.

The afternoon's accounting was patient. Altuve's sixteenth home run had Houston ahead in the fourth, and ahead the Texans remained until the sixth, when Atlanta put four across in a single frame — the heart of them a three-run blast from Mike Yastrzemski, his twelfth of the year and his third of a road trip that went 4-and-2, with Albies driving home the fourth. A man bearing that name has hit October thunder before; the family trade continues. Mederos, in relief, took the decision at 5-and-1, Smith-Shawver and Kerr passed the late innings hand to hand, and Dodd sealed his second save, Diaz's eighth-inning blow the whole of Houston's answer. Four runs on six hits, not an error in the field — economy itself.

So the clinch this paper forecast Sunday morning arrived by Sunday evening, and by Atlanta's own hand: a 4-2 victory, a sweep of the Astros in their own park, and a seventh division title in the past nine years. "We've been fighting all year to get to this moment," said Pérez, and appended the sentence Atlanta will carry into October: "And we're not done yet." As the seedings stand this morning the Braves are the National's third seed, their Wild Card opponent to be drawn from among the Padres, Cubs, and Phillies — the arithmetic of that row is sorted at the October desk below. Houston's troubles, meanwhile, compound: a third straight defeat drops the Texans a game behind Texas in the West — the throne that has changed hands thrice in three mornings stays with Arlington a second day, both claimants having lost — and their grip on the wild-card row is now three games short of Chicago's chair with six to play.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: BOSTON CLINCHES BY LOSING, TAMPA BAY MAKES A FORTRESS OF ITS DOME — AND THE CROWN MAY PASS THROUGH THE BRONX AS SOON AS TOMORROW

The strangest celebration of the year unfolded in the visitors' clubhouse at St. Petersburg, where the Red Sox — beaten 5-1 by the Rays an hour earlier — learned that Houston's defeat at Atlanta had punched their postseason ticket regardless, and set the Bee Gees' "Stayin' Alive" playing on what witnesses describe as an endless loop. A club that spent its first three months among the American's also-rans is October-bound; the berth is the reward of the long climb back, and no man in the room apologized for the scoreboard's assistance.

Their hosts, meanwhile, closed the home ledger in state. Tampa Bay's 5-1 decision was its five-and-fiftieth victory of the year in the rebuilt dome — a single-season record for the house — capping an 8-and-1 homestand that included three walk-off victories. The East's lead stands at six with seven to play, and the arithmetic now runs through the Bronx: the Rays need but one victory in the four-game set at Yankee Stadium that opens with Tuesday's doubleheader to wear the division's crown and the league's first seed. In the National, the row beneath the champions re-sorts nightly: the Cubs and Padres sit level at seven-and-eighty wins, Chicago holding the row's head by its season series against both San Diego and Philadelphia; the Padres — winners of thirteen of fourteen, the hottest club in the land — carry a magic number of two toward a third consecutive postseason, a thing never once managed in the franchise's eight-and-fifty seasons; and Milwaukee, its franchise record already banked as the card below relates, needs but one more victory — or one more Atlanta defeat — to claim the National's first-round bye. Both clubs stand idle this day, so that question keeps until Tuesday.

THE MILESTONE DESK: TWENTY-AND-TWENTY, TWICE OVER — CHOURIO WRITES A LINE NO MAN HIS AGE EVER WROTE, AND CRUZ JOINS BONDS AND McCUTCHEN IN THE PITTSBURGH BOOK

History was made at Camden Yards by way of a walk and a dash. When Jackson Chourio stole second in the sixth inning Sunday — safe upon appeal to the moving pictures, the first call having gone against him — the theft was his twentieth of the season, set beside four-and-twenty home runs, and made him the first player in Major League history to complete three 20-20 campaigns before his twenty-third birthday. Only Julio Rodríguez of Seattle and Bobby Witt Jr. of Kansas City have so much as opened their careers with three straight such seasons, and neither did it so young. "That's just Chourio," shrugged his old bush-league mate Misiorowski. "He's an animal out there." The Wonder Kid stole another base later in the evening for good measure.

And at Pittsburgh, Oneil Cruz heard the two names he had just joined and paused a full ten seconds before speaking. His fourth-inning blast off Wacha — a 75-mile-an-hour curveball dispatched 420 feet to dead center — was his twentieth home run, making him merely the third Pirate ever to pair twenty homers with twenty steals in three consecutive seasons. The others are Barry Bonds and Andrew McCutchen. That Cruz has done it in three-and-ninety games, two months of his summer lost to a fractured hand, only sharpens the figure; since his August return he bats .318 and slugs .533, and his club — 52-and-41 with him, 27-and-36 without — has won four straight, as the card relates.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: A FOUL BALL FINDS THE MAN WAITING HIS TURN — BREGMAN CARTED TO THE HOSPITAL FROM THE ON-DECK CIRCLE, AND TORONTO'S SICK LIST LENGTHENS BY TWO

The ugliest moment of the Sunday card involved no pitch thrown in anger. In the fourth inning at Cincinnati, Alex Bregman stood in the on-deck circle when his teammate Busch half-swung at an offering from Mey and fouled it squarely into Bregman's left cheekbone. The third baseman walked to the dugout under his own power, was lifted for a pinch-hitter, and was sent to the hospital for X-rays and further examination; the club had no verdict by night's end. "Any time the ball hits the head area, it's scary," said Busch, who bore the guiltless guilt of the man at the plate. "You focus on the game, but it's tough." The Cubs won the game 9-1, and would trade the margin entire for a clean bill.

Toronto's troubles wear no bandage so visible but run deeper into the pitching ledger. Dylan Cease, the staff's ace, has been sent back to Toronto for an examination of his throwing shoulder and is scratched from his Wednesday turn, the club awaiting the pictures before speaking of a return; and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. left Sunday's victory at Arlington in the fourth inning with tightness of the lower back — "we just wanted to be careful," said the manager Schneider, "and hopefully he's good for tomorrow." For a club three games shy of the wild-card row's last chair, every man on the table is a game off the ledger.

THE CONVALESCENT DESK: WEDNESDAY IS NAMED FOR THE GREAT RETURN — OHTANI'S SHELF-LEAVE EXPIRES MIDWEEK, WHILE SKUBAL STEPS AWAY ON A FAMILY MATTER AND THE CHAMPIONS SHUFFLE THEIR DECK

The vigil this paper has kept over Shohei Ohtani's recovery may close midweek. The manager Roberts, having promised Saturday that the returning series was at hand, has now named the day: there is "a good chance" the great man is activated Wednesday, when his fifteen-day shelf-leave — dated back to the eighth of September — expires, in the second game of San Diego's visit to Chavez Ravine. He returns strictly as a batsman, the mound closed for his year, and the swings taken against the pitching-machine that throws like a big-leaguer have all come away satisfactory.

The same champions spent Sunday shuffling the deck around him. Tarik Skubal went to the bereavement list on a family matter — "he's fine," Roberts assured, and the leave may cost him no turn at all, his next start projected for Friday at San Francisco — while Sheehan and Hurt came up from Oklahoma City, and Sheehan promptly struck out nine Giants across a long scoreless relief, as the card below admires. Tucker, nursing a leg bruised by his own foul ball Saturday, sat the start and then pinch-hit anyway. The champions won their fourth straight all the same; whole in October is the only wholeness they are counting.

THE BROADCAST BOOTH: KUIPER TAKES THE HARD NEWS STANDING — A SECOND BOUT WITH CANCER ANNOUNCED, AND A VOW TO CALL HIS OLD FRIEND'S FAREWELL

Sad tidings from the Bay, borne with the steadiness of a man who has sat before a microphone for decades. Duane Kuiper, six-and-seventy years old and the voice of the Giants for a generation, announced Sunday that he has been diagnosed with throat cancer — an illness unrelated, his physicians say, to the cancer he fought and beat in 2021 — and that treatment at Stanford began last week. "I'm optimistic that it will be successfully treated," he said, and the paper takes him at his word.

The timing is its own small heartbreak: the booth beside him belongs to Mike Krukow, his friend of forty years, who retires when this season ends after six-and-thirty years behind the microphone. Kuiper had hoped to call the weekend's games at Los Angeles and could not travel; he plans instead to return to the booth Tuesday, and to call the season's closing series against the Dodgers at Oracle Park — the sendoff, he means to say, will not go unvoiced. The Herald, which trades daily in the sound of the game, tips its hat to a man who has supplied so much of it, and wishes him the swift and total recovery the record says he knows how to make.

The Rest of the Card

SÁNCHEZ BANKS AN EIGHTEENTH AND SCHWARBER WALKS FOUR TIMES WITHOUT SWINGING AT ANYTHING USEFUL — THE QUAKERS TAKE THE FLUSHING FINALE: QUAKERS 7, METS 2

Cristopher Sánchez worked deep into the evening for his eighteenth victory against six defeats, while Philadelphia's patience did the scoring — nine walks drawn in all, four of them by Schwarber alone — and Crawford tripled and drove home three. Bichette's seventeenth home run supplied the whole of the Flushing answer; the Quakers hold the National's third wild-card chair, one game astern of the row's co-leaders, with the champions of Milwaukee arriving Tuesday.

CRUZ'S TWENTIETH IN THE FOURTH, FLORES JR.'S ANSWER IN THE EIGHTH — THE BUCS SWEEP KANSAS CITY AND MAKE IT FOUR STRAIGHT: BUCS 4, ROYALS 3

Pasquantino's two-run blow in the seventh had put Kansas City ahead 3-2, whereupon the rookie Rafael Flores Jr. struck a two-run homer in the eighth — his tenth — to take it back for good. Cruz's milestone thunder, enshrined at the desk above, had kept the ledger close; Mlodzinski took the decision and Montgomery sealed his sixteenth save, and Pittsburgh, at nine-and-seventy wins with six to play, is assembling a September nobody asked its permission for.

NINE STRIKEOUTS, THREE HITS, AND THE STRIKEOUT CROWN RECLAIMED — WILLIAMS SENDS THE CLEVELAND NINE HOME IN FRONT: CLEVELAND NINE 1, ATHLETICS 0

Gavin Williams gave seven innings of three hits and a lone walk, struck out nine to retake the American's strikeout lead, and left the rest to Adell — whose fourth-inning knock drove home run number three-and-ninety of his season, the game's only tally — and to Smith, whose nine-and-thirtieth save closed the sweep. "You can kind of see the panic in a lot of the hitters," observed Kwan. Five straight victories send Cleveland on the road holding the Central by one over Chicago; the Athletics, whitewashed, have dropped six straight.

FOUR IN THE FIRST AND THE DOME'S LEDGER CLOSES AT FIVE-AND-FIFTY — THE SUNSHINE NINE BID THEIR HOUSE FAREWELL IN STATE: SUNSHINE NINE 5, CRIMSON HOSE 1

Tampa Bay fell upon Sandoval for four runs before the first inning was out — DeLuca and Simpson driving home two apiece, Mesa Jr. adding his fourteenth homer later — and Jax with five relief hands behind him kept Boston to a single ninth-inning run on Story's fifth. The victory was the record fifty-fifth in the dome this season and the defeated clinched anyway, as the October desk relates — a game whose loser left in champagne, which even this correspondent's archives cannot precedent. Simpson's stolen base was his six-and-fortieth.

A TRIPLE SHY OF THE CYCLE AND TWO SHY OF FORTY-AND-FORTY — CROW-ARMSTRONG'S FIVE-AND-FORTIETH POWERS THE ROUT AT CINCINNATI: CUBS 9, REDLEGS 1

Pete Crow-Armstrong, hitless the two days prior, answered with three hits — single, double, and his five-and-fortieth home run, the triple alone withheld — stole his eight-and-thirtieth base to stand two thefts from the first 40-40 season in the franchise book, and drove in two of Chicago's nine. Suzuki's five-and-twentieth and Conforto's fifteenth joined the barrage; Peterson took his ninth win; Bregman's run-scoring single preceded the misfortune the infirmary ward records, and the Cubs' clinch-watch continues, Arizona's victory having kept the champagne corked a day.

THE RAIN DELAY OUTLASTED THE BASEBALL, AND THE BASEBALL WAS ALL CHICAGO'S — MEIDROTH'S THUNDER KEEPS THE LAST CHAIR WARM: WHITE STOCKINGS 8, BENGALS 1

The crowd waited out three hours and fifty minutes of weather to see two hours and fifty of baseball, and the White Stockings made the arithmetic worth it: Meidroth homered and drove in two, Antonacci matched him with two of his own and a stolen base besides, and Murakami and Grichuk added knocks in a ten-hit evening while Detroit managed a single late run. Brazobán took the decision in relief. Chicago thus holds the American's final wild-card chair by three over Toronto and Houston, one game off Cleveland's Central lead — every road still open.

HERRERA STRIKES TWICE AND THE BOY BERNAL BREAKS IT LATE — A THREE-RUN EIGHTH SENDS THE CAPITAL NINE HOME EMPTY: REDBIRDS 5, CAPITAL NINE 3

Iván Herrera homered twice — his seventeenth and eighteenth — yet Washington stood a run ahead entering the eighth, whereupon St. Louis put three across, Bernal's fourth home run the loudest of the blows. Gastelum took the decision and O'Brien sealed his eight-and-thirtieth save, most in the National; Abrams answered for Washington with his one-and-thirtieth homer and three-and-thirtieth steal in a losing cause.

FOUR IN THE SEVENTH UNDO deGROM AND THE SWEEP IS AVOIDED — TORONTO'S CANDLE GUTTERS BUT DOES NOT GO OUT: BLUE JAYS 7, RANGERS 2

Toronto nicked single runs through the early innings, absorbed Burger's two-run seventh-and-twentieth homer, and then broke the thing open with four in the seventh — McAdoo and Lukes driving home two apiece on the night, Clement's two-and-thirtieth double among eleven Toronto hits. Arrighetti took the decision in relief; deGrom was charged with his tenth defeat against eleven victories. The Jays, three back of the last chair, stay mathematically breathing — though Guerrero's fourth-inning exit, recorded at the infirmary ward, shadowed the win. Texas, beaten, keeps the West's throne by a game only because Houston fell the same afternoon.

SEVEN SCORELESS IN THE MOUNTAIN AIR FROM A MAN A MONTH IN THE LEAGUE — ANDERSON MAKES COORS FIELD SIT QUIETLY: SEATTLE NINE 2, ROCKIES 1

Kade Anderson, called up only in late August, gave the start of his young life where pitching goes to die: seven innings at Denver, three hits, no walks, seven strikeouts, not a run, and all of it on four-and-eighty pitches. Canzone drove home both Seattle runs; Goodman's nine-and-thirtieth homer in the ninth spoiled the whitewash before Bazardo banked his first save. The Rockies' ninety-ninth defeat leaves them a game from the century; Seattle plays out the string with its eyes openly on 2027 — "and beyond," as the wires put it.

TWO HITS ARE ALL ANAHEIM CAN SHOW FOR NINE INNINGS — KREMER AND OBER PASS THE WHITEWASH BETWEEN THEM, AND RODEN DRIVES HOME FOUR: TWIN CITIES NINE 8, SERAPHS 0

Kremer carried the shutout deep and Ober carried it home, two Anaheim hits the entire evening's yield, while Minnesota's thirteen hits included the young Roden's first home run of the campaign in a four-run night's work, Bell driving home two more and the rookie Ross logging his first steal and first run driven in of the season besides. The Twin Cities men square their account at the season's margin; the Seraphs absorb defeat six-and-ninety, whitewashed a second time in three nights.

CRONENWORTH TWICE, TATIS ONCE, AND THE DRUM ROLLS ON — THIRTEEN WINS IN FOURTEEN, AND THE MAGIC NUMBER READS TWO: PADRES 7, MARLINS 3

Jake Cronenworth homered twice and drove in five — a season's work in an evening — and Tatis added his five-and-twentieth as San Diego banked a fifth consecutive victory, Buehler taking the decision. Sanoja's three-run seventh-inning homer was the whole of Miami's reply. The Friars' arithmetic is entered at the October desk: no club in the land is hotter, and no Padres club in eight-and-fifty years has reached October three years running — a drought two victories from its end.

FOUL BY FEET, THEN FAIR BY PLENTY — ARENADO'S SECOND-CHANCE SLAM OVERTURNS THE AFTERNOON, AND THE DESERT NINE REFUSE THE UNDERTAKER A DAY LONGER: DESERT NINE 8, YANKEES 4

New York's third inning produced three home runs nose to tail — Ramos, the boy Lombard Jr., and Jones — and a 4-1 lead that lasted precisely until Nolan Arenado came up with the bases full in the fifth. His first blast hooked foul at the pole; the next pitch he hammered fair into the left-field seats — a grand slam, his ninth of a career and third of the season, tying the franchise's single-season record — crowning a five-run frame in the club's forty-seventh comeback victory of the year, most in the Majors. Perdomo tripled and drove home two more. The Desert nine remain four back of the last chair with six to play — alive, which was Sunday's entire object; the Yankees, still without their captain, dropped a second straight.

NINE STRIKEOUTS FROM THE MAN RECALLED AT NOON — SHEEHAN'S LONG RELIEF CARRIES THE ANGELENOS PAST THE BAY NINE: ANGELENOS 3, BAY NINE 1

Recalled from Oklahoma City in the morning's shuffle, Emmet Sheehan was in a big-league game by afternoon and struck out nine San Francisco batsmen across a long scoreless relief, the visitors' first-inning run standing alone all day. Los Angeles chipped a run apiece from the sixth, seventh, and eighth — Edman's seventh homer among them — with Bubic taking the decision and Scott his three-and-twentieth save. A fourth straight victory for the crowned champions of the West, who now await Wednesday's reinforcement as the convalescent desk relates; the Bay nine have lost two-and-ninety.

THREE INNINGS BY DESIGN FOR THE ACE, A RECORD BY RIGHT FOR THE CLUB — VICTORY EIGHT-AND-NINETY STANDS ALONE IN THE CREAM CITY BOOK: CREAM CITY NINE 3, ORIOLES 0

Misiorowski threw three sharp innings and departed exactly on schedule — nothing wrong, the club hastened to say, but a bringing-in of the great arm for its safe October landing — and six relief hands finished the whitewash, Hall taking the decision and Megill his nine-and-twentieth save. Contreras homered, the rookie shortstop Pratt singled home two, and Chourio ran into history as the milestone desk sings. Victory eight-and-ninety breaks the franchise record Milwaukee had only just tied, with six games yet to play and the first-round bye a single result away — the October desk holds that arithmetic.

The Monday tables, then — with two flags decided and a third near. In the American: Tampa Bay, its home ledger closed at a record five-and-fifty wins in the dome, leads clinched New York by six and may take the East with a single victory in the Bronx, where a doubleheader opens the four-game set Tuesday; the Central is Cleveland's by one over Chicago; the West is Texas's by one over Houston, both having lost Sunday, the Silver Boot tiebreaker still in Houston's keeping; and the wild-card row reads New York and Boston seated — Boston's ticket punched Sunday by Houston's defeat — with Chicago's last chair three clear of Toronto and Houston alike. In the National: Atlanta's East is sewn on, as the day's chief dispatch relates; Milwaukee, its franchise record standing at eight-and-ninety victories, needs one more win or one Atlanta defeat for the bye, and two more wins for the Central's first hundred-win season since the 2016 Cubs; the champions of the West have won four straight; and the wild-card row reads Cubs and Padres level at seven-and-eighty — Chicago's head chair held by the season series — with Philadelphia one back in the third and Arizona four adrift with six to play. Today's bill is a thin Monday card of three, verified against the schedule: Toronto at Baltimore at 6:35, Yesavage opposing Baz; Washington at Detroit at 6:40; and Minnesota at San Francisco at 9:45. Tomorrow the full board returns — the Bronx twin bill from 1:05, Milwaukee at Philadelphia with the bye perhaps in the balance, Cincinnati at Atlanta, and San Diego at Los Angeles with the Friars' magic number at two. Six mornings remain to the season's last page on the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: A MAN IN FULL FLIGHT OVER A CROUCHING CATCHER — LANGFORD LEAPS, DIVES BACK, AND TOUCHES THE WEST'S SUMMIT WITH HIS FINGERTIPS: RANGERS 6, BLUE JAYS 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 74 · Sunday, the Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

A MAN IN FULL FLIGHT OVER A CROUCHING CATCHER — LANGFORD LEAPS, DIVES BACK, AND TOUCHES THE WEST'S SUMMIT WITH HIS FINGERTIPS: RANGERS 6, BLUE JAYS 2

Six Arlington pitchers pass the evening hand to hand, Montgomery's three and two-thirds without a hit taking the decision; Jung's first-inning thunder and a three-run sixth undo Soriano's eight strikeouts; and with Houston falling at home, Texas wakes alone atop the American's West — the third different top line in three mornings

The picture the wires will carry from Arlington is of Wyatt Langford airborne. Sixth inning, Langford at third, Evan Carter's fly ball settling into the center fielder's glove — the tag, the sprint, and there at the plate crouched the catcher Kirk, squarely in the baseline. Langford did not slide. He hurdled the man entire, sailed past the plate in the doing of it, and had to dive back and touch it by hand before the pitcher Sewald, covering, could apply the tag. "Just put my head down and ran," the young man explained afterward, as though describing a trip to the post office. "He ended up being down in the baseline. It just kinda all happened. I didn't really plan on doing all that."

The run he stole out of the air crowned a three-run sixth that broke the game open, and the evening's arithmetic was every bit as acrobatic. Texas made six runs of five hits: Jung's eleventh home run on the game's first turn through the order, two more in the second on Giménez's throwing error and a wild pitch, then the sixth — Langford's run-scoring double, Jansen struck by a pitch with the bases full, and Carter's sacrifice fly with its famous conclusion. Toronto's Soriano struck out eight and was brilliant for five innings, yet the ledger charged him six runs; such is September's bookkeeping. The Arlington men, for their part, made the whole night a relay — six pitchers, the opener Quantrill handing the ball to Montgomery, whose three and two-thirds innings without a hit earned the decision, Eovaldi and three others carrying it home. Kirk's run-scoring single and Schneider's solo blow were the whole of Toronto's answer, and the Jays, three games shy of the wild-card row's last chair with their candle guttering, dropped a second straight.

And so the West has now shown a different face on three consecutive mornings: Houston alone at the summit Friday, a dead heat Saturday, and this morning Texas alone — eight-and-seventy wins to Houston's seven-and-seventy, the Astros having fallen to Atlanta as the card below relates. One caution attends the celebration: the Silver Boot tiebreaker remains in Houston's keeping, so the Rangers must finish clear rather than level. Seven games remain to each. The same clubs resume this afternoon at 2:35, with deGrom taking the ball for Texas, and the desk observes that a man who will leap a catcher in September may be trusted to keep his head down in October.

News Around the League

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE CAPTAIN SPEAKS FROM THE SHELF — JUDGE CALLS THE CALF SETBACK FRUSTRATING BUT HOLDS TO THE PLAN: "I'D LIKE TO BE BACK BY THE POSTSEASON"

A day after the ten-day shelving this paper recorded Saturday, Aaron Judge stood before the Phoenix press and named the injury's fine print: the strain sits in the soleus muscle of the right calf — "a little more crucial with running and hitting," by the captain's own anatomy lesson — and he allowed that it differs from the calf troubles he has managed through seasons past. The frustration was plain; the resolve was plainer. "I'd like to be back by the postseason," he said. "That's definitely the plan."

The ledger behind the words is a hard one. Judge had appeared in just six games since his return from the fractured rib on the eighth of September, going 4-for-23 with a single home run before the calf lifted him from Wednesday's game in Minneapolis, and the manager Boone continues to decline any grading of the strain's severity — the stated focus is simply October readiness. His mates split the difference in his absence at Phoenix, as the card below sorrowfully relates.

THE CONVALESCENT DESK: THE MACHINE THAT THROWS LIKE A BIG-LEAGUER MEETS THE MAN WHO HITS LIKE NO ONE ELSE — OHTANI TAKES FORTY SWINGS, RUNS THE BASES, AND ROBERTS NAMES THE SERIES OF HIS RETURN

The champions' great convalescent advanced another station on Saturday. Shohei Ohtani, whose progression to coach-pitched batting practice this paper entered only yesterday, graduated to the Trajekt machine — the contraption that conjures live big-league pitching from film — took thirty to forty swings, ran the bases during batting practice besides, and "came away feeling good," by the manager Roberts' account. Then Roberts said the thing the whole of Los Angeles has waited a fortnight to hear: "There's a good chance next series we'll see him."

The calendar makes the promise specific. The next series is San Diego's visit to Chavez Ravine, opening Tuesday — the season's final home engagement — and the fifteen-day list, dated back to the eighth of September, releases him Wednesday at the earliest. He returns strictly as a batsman, the mound finished for his year, carrying a .902 on-base-plus-slugging figure and thirty home runs into the recovery; the champions have somehow gone 13-3 across their last sixteen without him, and now propose to be whole for October.

THE MILESTONE DESK: A CHECK-SWING BUNT DETHRONES THE POLAR BEAR — BENGE'S HUNDRED SIX-AND-FIFTIETH HIT IS A NEW METS ROOKIE MARK, AND VARGAS WRITES A LINE NO WHITE STOCKING EVER WROTE

Record-breaking has rarely looked so humble. In the eighth inning at Flushing, Carson Benge — who had already put a home run into the right-field seats off Painter, his nineteenth — dribbled a check-swing bunt down the third-base line and legged out hit number one hundred six-and-fifty, passing Pete Alonso's franchise rookie mark of one hundred five-and-fifty. "It's special to see the guys that have come through here, all the greats," said the young man, who has answered the bell in 149 of the club's 155 games and sits within reach of the franchise rookie stolen-base mark besides, with two-and-twenty thefts. "He's just a baseball player," offered the interim manager Green, "which is one of the best compliments you can give somebody." The wires note for scale that the Major League rookie figure remains Ichiro Suzuki's 242, a mountain visible from every foothill.

And on the South Side, Miguel Vargas stole his twentieth base in the evening's victory and thereby completed a season's line no White Sox player has ever written: thirty doubles, thirty home runs, twenty steals, and a hundred runs scored in the same campaign. His three-and-thirtieth homer, struck the same night, stands in the card below — the milestone and the pennant race carrying the same man's signature.

THE OCTOBER DESK: TAMPA BAY WALKS OFF A THIRD TIME AND THE CROWN COMES NEARER — ATLANTA MAY SEW ON THE EAST THIS VERY AFTERNOON, MILWAUKEE TIES ITS OWN RECORD, AND THE NATIONAL'S WILD-CARD ROW RE-SORTS ITSELF

The Rays have made a habit of the last word. Palacios' ninth-inning knock — sung in the card below — was Tampa Bay's third walk-off victory of this final homestand, a thing the club had not managed since September of 2019, and its thirty-ninth come-from-behind win of the year, most in the American. Seven victories in eight games have stretched the East's lead to five over New York with eight remaining, and the first division crown since 2021 is close enough to touch.

In the National, the clinchings queue up. Atlanta, six clear of Philadelphia with seven to play after Acuña's thunder at Houston, may seal a seventh East title in nine seasons this very afternoon — any Braves victory or Phillies defeat does it. Crowned Milwaukee's 1-0 jewel at Baltimore was victory seven-and-ninety, drawing the club level with its own franchise record set only last season, and the magic number for the National's first-round bye stands at two. And the wild-card row, a three-way dead heat only yesterday, has re-sorted itself: the Cubs and Padres sit level at six-and-eighty wins — Chicago holding the row's head by the season series — with San Diego alone in the second chair, Philadelphia a game astern in the third after its drubbing at Flushing, and Arizona, refusing to die, four back with seven to play. In the American, Chicago's grip on the final chair is two games over Houston, whose evening is weighed in the card below, with Toronto three back.

THE CLUBHOUSE DESK: THE WALL WINS NOTHING — CAGLIANONE OWNS HIS TEMPER, TAKES HIS BENCHING, AND ANSWERS WITH THE TYING KNOCK

Contrition, then redemption, in the space of two days. Jac Caglianone, three-and-twenty years old and in his first full campaign, punched a dugout wall during Thursday's defeat at Houston and cut his left hand — no serious damage, the club reports — whereupon the manager Quatraro sat him Friday as a matter of discipline. The young man did not hide behind the trainer's report. "It was a very selfish and immature move on my part," he said, adding that "these guys hold me to a higher standard." The frustration had roots: a 0-for-10 skid with eight strikeouts across his previous seven games, in a season that otherwise reads .279 with three-and-twenty homers.

Restored to the lineup Saturday as the designated hitter, he made the apology material: a seventh-inning single that squared the game at Pittsburgh, the go-ahead run scored a moment later, and his seventh stolen base besides. That his club let the evening slip late — the card below has the arithmetic — takes nothing from the lesson: the wall teaches only what the bat can unteach.

The Rest of the Card

BURKE HOLDS THE LINE AND VARGAS SIGNS THE EVENING TWICE — THE PALE HOSE ANSWER FRIDAY'S HEARTBREAK AND KEEP EVERY RACE ALIVE: PALE HOSE 3, MOTOR CITY NINE 1

A night after eight runs went for nothing, Chicago played the tidy hand: Sean Burke gave six innings of one run for his tenth victory — his first six-inning turn since the one-and-twentieth of August — and Miguel Vargas struck his three-and-thirtieth homer and stole the milestone base the desk above enshrines. Taylor sealed his tenth save, and the Pale Hose remain one behind Cleveland in the Central while holding the American's last wild-card chair by two; the same clubs settle the series this afternoon.

ONE RUN ON A GROUNDOUT, AND GASSER MAKES IT A FORTRESS — VICTORY SEVEN-AND-NINETY TIES THE FRANCHISE BOOK: SUDS MEN 1, BIRDS 0

Robert Gasser threw a career-high 107 pitches across seven scoreless innings, three hits the whole of Baltimore's take against him, and the game's lone run crossed in the second on the humblest of instruments — Ortiz tripling and trotting home on Sánchez's groundout. Uribe and Ashby closed the whitewash, and Milwaukee's seven-and-ninetieth victory draws the club level with its own franchise record, the bye arithmetic standing at two as the October desk counts. Spare a line for the loser: Baltimore's Trevor Rogers struck out ten across eight innings of three-hit ball and was beaten anyway — September keeps a cruel ledger.

BELLO FANS ELEVEN AND LOSES TO A POPUP — PALACIOS DROPS THE SOFTEST HIT OF THE NIGHT WHERE NO GLOVE LIVES, AND THE TRADE IS A THIRD WALK-OFF: RAYS 2, RED SOX 1

Boston's Bello was magnificent — eight innings, five hits, eleven strikeouts, not a walk — and Tampa Bay's Peralta answered with six strikeouts of his own, Aranda's two-and-twentieth squaring Anthony's early run-scoring double. Then the ninth: two out, runners at the corners, and Richie Palacios lifted a 65.7-mile-an-hour popup off Whitlock that fell into shallow right field like a leaf, Caminero scoring the winner unearned. "Just praying it drops. That's all you're doing," said the honest hero; the crown arithmetic his prayer advanced is entered at the October desk.

A RECORD IN THE MORNING COLUMNS, TEN RUNS IN THE EVENING LEDGER — ALVAREZ'S THREE-RUN TURN AND A FOUR-RUN EIGHTH SEND PHILADELPHIA TO THE THIRD CHAIR: FLUSHING NINE 10, PHILS 3

Down 3-1 in the fifth, the Flushing men answered with Francisco Alvarez's three-run homer, two more in the sixth, and a four-run eighth built of walks and singles pressed nose to tail against a parade of Philadelphia relievers. Carson Benge homered and then broke the franchise rookie hit record by bunt, as the milestone desk celebrates; Painter took the defeat, his tenth, and the Phils fell out of the wild-card deadlock into its third chair, five games of East arithmetic now against them with Atlanta able to clinch this very day.

FOUR HITS, TWO THUNDERCLAPS FROM EITHER SIDE OF THE PLATE, AND A TRIPLE SHY OF THE CYCLE — MARTÍNEZ RETURNS FROM THE SHELF SWINGING: LAKE ERIE MEN 12, WHITE ELEPHANTS 6

Angel Martínez, five days an invalid, came back with four hits and eleven total bases — a home run from each side of the plate, a double, a single, four runs driven home, and only the triple withheld from a cycle. DeLauter's three-run first-inning blow erased an early deficit, four consecutive doubles decorated a five-run third, and Cleveland's fourth straight victory holds the Central's lead at one over Chicago; the Athletics' Walton drove in four in a losing cause. "The offense is clicking at the right time," said the manager Vogt, in what the standings suggest is understatement.

BOYD BANKS HIS NINTH AND THE LATE THUNDER KEEPS THE ROW'S HEAD — BUSCH'S TWENTIETH AND SWANSON'S NINETEENTH BOOKEND A TIDY EVENING: NORTH SIDERS 5, QUEEN CITY NINE 2

Chicago nicked runs in five different innings — Shaw's sacrifice fly, Suzuki's single, then Michael Busch's twentieth homer to break a 2-2 tie in the sixth, Hoerner's knock and Dansby Swanson's nineteenth for insurance — while Boyd took his ninth victory despite Cincinnati's two-run fifth, Rolison sealing his third save. The North Siders thus keep the head of the National's wild-card row by the season series over San Diego, as the October desk sorts; the Reds managed four hits all night.

LOWE'S THREE-AND-THIRTIETH ARRIVES WITH THE GAME IN THE BALANCE — PITTSBURGH SHRUGS OFF A BLOWN LEAD AND BANKS A THIRD STRAIGHT: BUCCANEERS 6, ROYALS 5

Kansas City clawed from 4-1 down to 5-4 ahead — Caglianone's tying knock and go-ahead run the clubhouse desk's whole sermon — only for Brandon Lowe to answer in the eighth with a two-run homer, his three-and-thirtieth, that restored the lead for good. Simon's first homer of the year and Mangum's fifth had built the early cushion; Jensen's five-and-twentieth for Kansas City survived a review; Montgomery sealed his fifteenth save, and the Buccaneers, winners of three straight, stand a game above .500 at eight-and-seventy wins.

ACUÑA EMPTIES THE BASES WITH ONE SWING AND THE WEST'S THRONE EMPTIES WITH IT — HOUSTON'S HOLD ON FIRST LASTS EXACTLY ONE MORNING: BRAVES 6, ASTROS 3

Trailing 2-1 in the seventh with the bases full, Ronald Acuña Jr. turned on a 96.9-mile-an-hour fastball from Abreu and deposited it in the left-center seats — a grand slam, his twentieth homer, four runs driven in, and the sixth blow of a September in which he bats .373. "It's the best feeling ever when a guy is throwing 96 or 97 and you get it," said the great man. "You don't feel anything." Holmes gave six innings of two for his tenth victory and Iglesias sealed number four-and-thirty; Paredes drove in two of Houston's runs and scored the third on Diaz's late double, and the defeat — a ninth in thirteen games — dropped the Astros from the summit they had held a single morning. "It's go time," said Walker of the six road games that close the season after this afternoon's home finale; the manager Espada was terser: "We have to really flush this one quick."

ELEVEN INNINGS, SIX ERRORS, AND A RUN FORCED HOME BY THE CATCHER'S GLOVE — WASHINGTON WINS THE UNTIDIEST GAME OF THE NIGHT: WASHINGTONS 8, MOUND CITY NINE 5

Lile's two-run homer opened the scoring and then the game descended into glorious disorder — six errors between the clubs, St. Louis twice pulling level late, a tenth inning traded run for run — until the eleventh, when a challenge overturned the call at the plate and Jacob Young was awarded catcher's interference with the bases full, forcing home the lead run. Tena's two-run double and Crews' sacrifice fly made it a four-run frame; Cornelio took the decision and Dion banked his first save. The desk also notes, for the almanac's sake, that the rival shortstops Nuñez and Winn passed the evening's idle moments at tic-tac-toe — September baseball in one image.

ON THE NIGHT ARIZONA TOASTED 2001, A PINCH-HITTER SUPPLIES THE SEQUEL — PAVIN SMITH'S TWO-RUN THUNDER IN THE NINTH KEEPS THE LONGEST SHOT ALIVE: SONORAN NINE 5, PINSTRIPES 3

With the 2001 champions gathered at Chase Field for their five-and-twentieth anniversary, the evening demanded drama and got it: Schlittler carried a no-hitter into the fifth before Lawlar's two-run triple, New York answered through Ramos and Wells in the sixth, and in the ninth — a strike-three call on Vargas having been overturned by challenge a moment before — Pavin Smith, a man designated for assignment in July and rebuilt in Reno, struck a two-run walk-off homer off Fulmer. "We know what we have to do. Our backs are against the wall," said the manager Lovullo, four back of the last chair with seven to play. The Pinstripes, still without their captain, remain five behind Tampa Bay.

RALEIGH AND AROZARENA STRIKE EARLY, AND DENVER TAKES THE REST OF THE EVENING BACK — A FOUR-RUN SEVENTH IN THE MOUNTAIN AIR: MOUNTAIN MEN 5, M'S 3

Raleigh's two-run blow in the first and Arozarena's six-and-twentieth had Seattle ahead by three, but the visitors' gloves gave the game away by degrees — three errors in all — and Colorado's seventh did the arithmetic: McCarthy's groundout, Rumfield's single, and Cole Carrigg's two-run knock, four runs in the frame. Mejia took the decision and Bernardino sealed his second save; for the Mountain men it is merely a seven-and-fiftieth victory in a season of eight-and-ninety defeats, but the home crowd cheered it like June.

TWENTY YEARS OLD, BASES FULL, TENTH INNING — SALAS SINGLES HOME THE WINNER AND SAN DIEGO SEIZES THE SECOND CHAIR ALONE: FRIARS 7, FISH 6, IN TEN INNINGS

Miami led 5-1 by the third and Conine's ninth-inning homer squared the game at six, but the tenth belonged to the youngest man on the field: Ethan Salas, the twenty-year-old catcher called up at September's start, laced a bases-loaded single to center to score Cronenworth — the youngest player to deliver a walk-off hit since Manny Machado in September of 2012. "You got 50,000 going ballistic for you and the boys ready for you if everything works out. It definitely felt awesome," said the youth. Tatis' four-and-twentieth had tied it earlier; twelve victories in thirteen games now, and the Friars hold the National's second wild-card chair alone, level with the Cubs at the row's head, as the October desk sorts.

THREE DOUBLES FOR BETTS IN A FOUR-HIT SIZZLE — THE CHAMPIONS SCORE IN SIX STRAIGHT INNINGS AND SKUBAL BANKS HIS ELEVENTH: TROLLEY DODGERS 10, JINTS 4

Mookie Betts collected four hits, three of them doubles, scored twice and drove in two — his September blaze rolling on — while Los Angeles put runs on the board in each of the first six innings, three-run frames in the fifth and sixth breaking it open with Smith's homer, Edman's two-run knock, and De Paula's pair along the way. Skubal weathered eight San Francisco hits across five innings for his eleventh victory, and four relievers finished without a run; Bericoto's two-run homer led the Jints, who have now dropped one-and-ninety games. The crowned champions, 13-3 in their last sixteen, await their convalescent as the desk above relates.

GRISSOM SQUARES IT IN THE NINTH AND MOORE ENDS IT IN THE ELEVENTH — THE ANAHEIM NINE OUTLAST MINNESOTA A SECOND STRAIGHT NIGHT: ANAHEIM NINE 6, NORTH STARS 5, IN ELEVEN INNINGS

Minnesota built leads of 3-0 and 5-2 — Keaschall doubling home the young Jenkins, Kreidler adding a solo blow — and watched both dissolve: Frazier's two-run double in the eighth, Vaughn Grissom's tying homer in the ninth, and at last, in the eleventh, Christian Moore's sharp ground ball off the pitcher Rogers that went for the winning single, Neto scoring and the venerable Trout pulling up at third as the run crossed. Saucedo took the decision against Rogers; a night after Minnesota's whitewash, the account is squared, and the same clubs close the set this afternoon.

The Sunday tables, then — with a new name atop the American's West. In the American: clinched Tampa Bay holds the East by five over clinched New York, Boston astern of both; the Central is Cleveland's by one over Chicago, the tiebreaker still Chicago's; and the West is Texas's alone by one over Houston, the Silver Boot tiebreaker in Houston's keeping, so the Rangers must finish clear. The wild-card row: New York and Boston seated, the last chair Chicago's by two over Houston, Toronto three back. In the National: Atlanta leads Philadelphia by six and may sew on the East this very afternoon — any Braves win or Phillies loss does it; crowned Milwaukee, level with its own franchise record at seven-and-ninety victories, holds a bye arithmetic of two; and the wild-card row reads Cubs and Padres level at six-and-eighty — Chicago's chair by the season series, San Diego's second alone — with Philadelphia one back and Arizona four adrift, seven to play. Today's bill is the full board of fifteen, verified against the schedule, and the desk commends: at 1:40 Boston at Tampa Bay; at 2:10 the clinch-watch at Houston, Pérez opposing Brown, and daylight baseball on the South Side, Melton against Martin; at 2:35 deGrom carries the West's new leaders against Toronto; at 4:10 the Yankees try to leave Phoenix with a split while Miami visits streaking San Diego; and at 7:20 Misiorowski — fifteen victories and an earned-run figure of 1.89 — takes the ball at Baltimore with the record-breaking eight-and-ninetieth victory on offer. Mark the almanac besides: tomorrow's card is a mere three games, the schedule catching its breath before the final week. Seven mornings remain to the season's last page on the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

The Herald Acknowledges Its Debts

entry.title: SIX UNEARNED RUNS SQUANDERED, NINE UNANSWERED RETURNED — DETROIT'S FIVE-RUN EIGHTH TURNS THE EVENING ON ITS HEAD, AND THE CENTRAL'S DEADLOCK BREAKS AGAINST CHICAGO: TIGERS 11, WHITE SOX 8
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 73 · Saturday, the Nineteenth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SIX UNEARNED RUNS SQUANDERED, NINE UNANSWERED RETURNED — DETROIT'S FIVE-RUN EIGHTH TURNS THE EVENING ON ITS HEAD, AND THE CENTRAL'S DEADLOCK BREAKS AGAINST CHICAGO: TIGERS 11, WHITE SOX 8

Hao-Yu Lee, whose fumble at third opened Chicago's six-run first, atones with four hits and the tying homer; McGonigle drives in four, three of them on the triple that sent Peters into a fence-pole; and with Cleveland winning by the lake, the White Sox wake a full game out of first with their wild-card cushion pared to one

The Tigers of Detroit will watch October from their parlors this autumn, which is precisely what makes them dangerous company in September: a club with nothing left to defend and every appetite for mischief. Chicago was taught the lesson by installments. The visitors nicked a run on a wild pitch in the first; the White Sox answered with six in the home half without earning a single one of them — a run home on a wild pitch of Sears' own, the door swung wide by Hao-Yu Lee's fumble at third, Colson Montgomery's three-run double and Vargas's knock among the traffic through nine batters. When Miguel Vargas added his two-and-thirtieth homer in the third, the count stood 8-2 and the evening had every look of a formality.

It was instead a slow confiscation. Kevin McGonigle singled home a run in the third, then emptied the bases in the fifth with a three-run triple to right-center — the drive on which the right fielder Peters, lunging and missing, met a fence-pole at a full run, as the ward below records — and Lee, of all men, set about repaying his error with interest: a run-scoring double in the sixth, then a two-run homer off Newcomb in the eighth that squared the account at eight apiece. Dingler's single put Detroit ahead, and Riley Greene's one-and-twentieth, two runs the richer, closed a five-run frame — nine unanswered runs in all. Sommers threw two perfect innings with five strikeouts for the victory; Jansen sealed his one-and-twentieth save. Lee's final ledger: four hits, a double, the tying homer, three driven in, and one error atoned in full.

Now the morning's arithmetic, which stings the South Side twice over. Cleveland won by the lake — the milestone desk sings the how of it — and so Friday morning's deadlock is Saturday's one-game Cleveland lead, nine-and-seventy wins to Chicago's eight-and-seventy. The tiebreaker remains Chicago's, the season series banked seven games to six, so the Cleveland men must still finish clear rather than level; but the White Sox' own cushion for the American's last wild-card chair is likewise down to a single game over Texas, and these same Tigers return to the South Side this very afternoon at ten past two. "Yeah, it's tough. No way about it," said the manager Venable. "Obviously you have a special first inning there and get the lead. Just weren't able to get any outs." Peters, nursing his bruises, spoke the professional's creed: "The only thing we can control is what we do tomorrow."

News Around the League

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE CAPTAIN OF THE YANKEES GOES BACK TO THE SHELF — JUDGE'S CALF STRAIN IS NAMED, WITH OCTOBER UNPROMISED; PETERS MEETS A FENCE-POLE; AND SAN FRANCISCO'S WEBB IS DONE FOR THE SEASON BY A BLISTER

The gravest cot belongs to the captain. The stiffness that lifted Aaron Judge from Wednesday's game in Minneapolis — entered in this paper's ward on Thursday — has a name now: a strain of the right calf, found by Thursday's examination in Phoenix, and it sends him to the ten-day invalid list this very day. The club will neither grade the strain's severity nor guess at a date, and the wires note that even the mildest of the kind commonly asks two or three weeks — with barely more than one remaining before October. Asked plainly whether his captain would return for the playoffs, the manager Boone answered: "I don't know. I don't have a timeline on him. I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires." What is certain is the cost in the near term: Judge misses the Phoenix weekend and the four-game engagement with Tampa Bay that opens Tuesday at his own Stadium, with the East itself in the balance. The utility man Schuemann travels to meet the club. "There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge," said Boone, "but we have high expectations. Those don't change now." His men made the words good for one night at least, as the card below relates.

The lesser cots: Chicago's Tristan Peters chased McGonigle's fifth-inning drive to right-center, missed it by a lunge, and struck a pole supporting the outfield fence at a full run; he lay on the grass a minute or two before leaving with the trainer, and the verdict — a contusion of the left shoulder and ribs, day to day — reads far kinder than the collision looked. And San Francisco has shelved Logan Webb, gone to the fifteen-day list with a blistered right middle finger, the stint dated back to Tuesday — arithmetic that quietly ends his regular season.

THE MILESTONE DESK: THE THOUSANDTH RUN DRIVEN HOME ARRIVES BY THUNDERCLAP — RAMÍREZ JOINS EARL AVERILL IN CLEVELAND'S OWN BOOK, AND OLSON'S FORTIETH CROWNS A CLINCHING NIGHT

In the sixth inning by the lake, with the Central's lead in the balance, José Ramírez struck a solo home run — the two hundred seven-and-ninetieth of his life, measured a foot past four hundred — and the run it drove home was the thousandth of his career. The house rose to him when the figure flashed upon the videoboard as he took his station at third in the seventh. Only Earl Averill, at one thousand four-and-eighty, has driven home more in all the franchise's annals, and among active players Ramírez — four-and-thirty years old as of Thursday — becomes just the twelfth man to the figure, joining a roll that includes Freeman, Goldschmidt, Arenado, Machado, and Trout. "I like to use those round numbers," said the manager Vogt. "Ten years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it's incredible what he has accomplished, and he's not even close to being done, right?" The second baseman Bazzana testified to the dugout's view: "We all looked at each other, and everyone's got a smile on their face. He's an incredible, incredible player." The milestone was no ornament, either — Ramírez also singled home the tying run an inning before his thunder, and the victory put Cleveland atop the Central alone, as the lead columns sing.

And at Houston, on the very night Atlanta punched its October ticket, Matt Olson struck a two-run blow in the ninth for his fortieth home run of the year — his second season of forty as a Brave, a company that holds only Hank Aaron with eight, Eddie Mathews with four, and Acuña and Andruw Jones with two apiece. Since 2018, the wires observe, only Schwarber, Judge, and Ohtani have struck more home runs than Olson's three hundred three. His center fielder Harris rendered the scouting report in full: "Yeah, he's pretty good."

THE OCTOBER DESK: ATLANTA PUNCHES AN EIGHTH TICKET IN NINE YEARS, THREE CLUBS SHARE THE NATIONAL'S WILD-CARD ROW TO THE DECIMAL, AND THE WEEKEND STANDS THICK WITH CLINCHINGS-IN-WAITING

The Braves are formally through the gate: Friday's victory at Houston, sung in the card below, clinched Atlanta a postseason berth for the eighth time in nine years. The clinching arm belonged to Tyler Mahle, whose earned-run figure since arriving from San Francisco at the deadline stands at 1.28 — third among all qualified starters since the fourth of August, behind only the Yankee Schlittler and Philadelphia's Luzardo. "It's just exciting to be part of such a good team," said the veteran, bound now for the first playoff start of his life. The East is not yet sewn on: Atlanta leads Philadelphia by five with eight to play, and to clinch the division before leaving Houston on Sunday night the Braves must sweep while the Phillies drop one of two at Flushing.

Beneath them, the National's wild-card row has closed to a dead heat of rare perfection: the Cubs and Phillies both lost, the Padres won an eleventh game in twelve, and all three now stand at five-and-eighty wins against nine-and-sixty defeats — three clubs, three chairs, the order a matter of tiebreakers alone, with San Diego seated third having lost both season series. Arizona, five back after a third straight defeat, is the only pursuer left with a case. And the clinchings queue up behind: Boston can seal its berth as early as this very day at Tampa Bay, other scoreboards consenting; San Diego can seal its own as soon as tomorrow; and crowned Milwaukee's magic number for the National's first-round bye — any combination of Brewer victories and Atlanta defeats — stands at three, with the club one win shy of its own franchise record of seven-and-ninety, set only last season, and two clear of the field for the game's best ledger.

THE CONVALESCENT DESK: GOOD BULLETINS FROM THE CHAMPIONS' WARD — SNELL WILL TAKE THE BALL AGAIN, OHTANI SWINGS AT COACH'S PITCHING, AND DÍAZ RETURNS TO FIGHT FOR A NINTH INNING OF HIS OWN

The Dodgers' invalid list, which has shadowed these columns all week, sent up three encouraging dispatches in a single day. Blake Snell, whose groin ended Wednesday's start after an inning, threw from ninety feet before Friday's game and came away well — no imaging was even ordered. "Happy that we caught it early," said the manager Roberts, who expects the left-hander to make one more regular-season start without limitation; since the eleventh of August his earned-run figure stands at 1.01 across seven turns. Shohei Ohtani took the next step of his own convalescence, hitting coach-pitched batting practice and emerging sound; he builds up strictly as a batsman — the mound is finished for his year — and the earliest the list releases him is Wednesday. Having stayed behind to mend while the flag was clinched at Cincinnati, the great man missed Thursday's champagne altogether; he will have to wait upon a deeper October toast.

And Edwin Díaz is back in uniform, activated from his second shelving of the season with the neck inflammation healed — the corresponding move sending down Landon Knack, the same man who banked four innings in Thursday's clincher, as this paper sang only yesterday; baseball's ledgers keep a cold sort of books. Díaz threw a scoreless ninth in the rout the card records, the fastball averaging 97.6 miles to the hour, a full tick above his season's figure. "The fastball had that life," said Roberts. "And then the slider — once you have that fastball, the slider is pretty lethal." The three-time All-Star, signed last winter to close, now auditions like any September hopeful for a place in the October bullpen. The champions rebuild themselves piece by piece, and the calendar just barely obliges.

THE BUSH-LEAGUE DESK: A SAVE, A STRIKEOUT, AND A PERFECT BACKFLIP — AMARILLO PUNCTUATES ITS PENNANT-CLINCHER IN THE GRAND MANNER

The desk closes among the bushes, where the Double-A Amarillo Sod Poodles — Arizona's outpost in the Texas League — punched their ticket to the league Finals with an 8-7 decision over Frisco on Friday night, one evening after erasing a six-run deficit with their season at the wall. The finishing flourish belonged to the right-hander Alfred Morillo, who recorded the game-ending strikeout to seal the save, ripped off his glove, and executed a perfect backflip in one unbroken motion; his catcher Barriga sprinted to the mound and the whole roster spilled out behind him. The wires reckon the left-hander Jefry Yan the reigning artist of the strikeout celebration, but concede this was something else entirely. Amarillo — whose ranks include Druw Jones, son of the same Andruw enshrined in the milestone desk's forty-homer company above — opens a best-of-three for the title against a Springfield club stocked with Cardinal prospects on Sunday, chasing a third Texas League crown in seven years. If a semifinal merits the backflip, the Herald trembles to imagine the choreography a pennant would loose.

The Rest of the Card

THE OPENER'S GAMBIT MISFIRES AND THE LONG MAN MENDS ALL — CANTILLO'S SIX SPOTLESS INNINGS CARRY THE FOREST CITY NINE TO THE SUMMIT ALONE: FOREST CITY NINE 5, ATHLETICS 3

Gelof greeted the opener Espino with a three-run homer before an out was recorded, and Cleveland spent the rest of the evening un-digging: Joey Cantillo gave six innings of two hits behind him for his tenth victory, Rocchio doubled two home in the fourth, José Ramírez singled the game level and then struck the milestone thunder the desk above enshrines, and Bazzana's fifteenth supplied the lead for good. Smith sealed his eight-and-thirtieth save. Three straight now for the Forest City nine, alone atop the Central by one — though the tiebreaker still wears a Chicago uniform, as the lead columns weigh.

THE THIRD PITCH OF THE EVENING TRAVELS FOUR HUNDRED EIGHT-AND-THIRTY FEET — ANTHONY DRIVES IN THREE, AND THE RAYS' STREAK DIES AT SIX: FENWAY MEN 4, RAYS 2

Roman Anthony tore into the third pitch of the night for a leadoff homer the machines measured at four hundred eight-and-thirty feet, then delivered his first career hit with the bases full — a two-run single an inning later — and Boston never trailed. Suarez carried one run into the sixth, and Miller, working around a bases-loaded ninth in which Simpson grounded out to end it, banked his fifth save. Tampa Bay went without a hit with runners in scoring position all night; the streak of six is dead, and the East's lead over New York is pared to four with the four-game reckoning at the Stadium opening Tuesday. The Fenway men, their bruised catcher still resting, may seal their October berth this very day, other scoreboards consenting.

SIX WALKS UNDO THE STRIKEOUT KING AND A NEW MAN THROWS FOUR SPOTLESS — THE RANGERS DRAW DEAD LEVEL ATOP THE WEST: RANGERS 7, MAPLE LEAF NINE 1

The heavyweight bill this desk commended on Friday came apart inside three innings: Dylan Cease, the American's strikeout sovereign, walked six men in two and two-thirds and was charged four runs — one of them earned, Toronto's three errors underwriting the rest — while Texas drew ten walks in all. Rocker labored through four and a third before Justin Williams threw four spotless innings for the victory; Burger doubled, drove in two, and the West is a dead heat at last, Houston and Texas level at seven-and-seventy wins and losses apiece with the Silver Boot tiebreaker in Houston's keeping. Texas also sits one game from Chicago's wild-card chair; the Maple Leaf nine slip two back with their candle guttering.

MAHLE CARVES SIX QUIET INNINGS AND THREE TWO-RUN THUNDERCLAPS DO THE REST — THE TOMAHAWK NINE SEAL AN EIGHTH OCTOBER IN NINE YEARS: TOMAHAWK NINE 6, ASTROS 2

Harris in the fourth, Acuña in the seventh, Olson in the ninth — each blow worth two runs, the last of them the fortieth the milestone desk celebrates — and Tyler Mahle made them stand with six innings of one run and six strikeouts on clinching night, as the October desk relates. Paredes drove in both Houston runs in a five-hit evening; the Astros have lost six of ten, and Friday's defeat dropped them into the .500 deadlock with Texas that now defines the West. Atlanta's East arithmetic — five up, a sweep-and-help scenario to clinch by Sunday — stands in the desk above.

CHOURIO'S OPENING STATEMENT, ALONSO'S ANSWER, AND A VERDICT DELIVERED IN THE TENTH — WIN SIX-AND-NINETY COMES THE HARD WAY: BREWERS 6, ORIOLES 5, IN TEN INNINGS

Jackson Chourio struck a three-run homer in the second and stole two bases besides — one theft shy now of a third consecutive twenty-twenty season — and Pete Alonso answered with a three-run blow of his own, upheld by the machines, for his eight-and-thirtieth. Milwaukee took the lead back in the ninth on Contreras' double and Yelich's single, watched Baltimore square it with two sacrifice flies off Megill — his first blown save since the fifth of June — and settled the matter in the tenth on Frelick's single, Patrick sealing it. Victory six-and-ninety stands one shy of the franchise record set only last season, and the bye arithmetic reads three, as the October desk counts.

THREE RUNS OFF THE OPENER BEFORE AN OUT WAS BOUGHT, THREE MORE FROM SOTO'S BAT — THE AMAZINS PULL PHILADELPHIA BACK INTO THE PACK: AMAZINS 6, PHILADELPHIAS 3

The opener Mayza surrendered three runs in a third of an inning, and the newly claimed José Urquidy — the waiver prize of Thursday's dealings desk — gave four and two-thirds scoreless with six strikeouts in a debut that deserved better company. Sosa's homer and double clawed Philadelphia within one before Juan Soto turned on Kerkering for a three-run homer, his six-and-twentieth, and Hill's eleventh closed the account. The defeat drops the Philadelphias into the three-way dead heat the October desk describes, five behind Atlanta in the East; the Amazins, long since out of the argument, collected thirteen hits and looked pleased with the spoiler's wages.

SKENES IS REACHED FOR FIVE AND THE SMOKY CITY NINE RALLY ROUND HIM — GRIFFIN'S FOUR HITS AND A THREE-RUN SEVENTH RESTORE THE LEDGER TO .500: SMOKY CITY NINE 8, ROYALS 5

Pasquantino and Massey both took Paul Skenes out of the yard, and the great arm left after six trailing — whereupon his mates paid the debt: Konnor Griffin collected four hits and two runs driven in, Lowe hammered his two-and-thirtieth with a man aboard, and a three-run seventh off Pearson — Horwitz singling home two, Griffin one — turned the evening for good. Ramírez took the decision, Soto sealed his fifteenth save, and Pittsburgh stands at seven-and-seventy wins and defeats alike, a .500 figure worn like a pressed suit in a lost year.

THE ACE IN MID-NEGOTIATION STATES HIS PRICE FROM THE MOUND — FIVE SCORELESS FROM CAVALLI AND SEVEN RUNS IN THREE INNINGS: SENATORS 9, CARDINALS 1

Cade Cavalli, whose contract-extension talks this paper entered only yesterday, argued his side of the table with five scoreless innings and six strikeouts for his thirteenth victory — a well-timed exhibit if ever the wires saw one. Dylan Crews' two-run homer crowned a seven-run burst across the first three innings off Leahy, and Washington cruised behind four doubles besides. St. Louis managed Herrera's late run and little else, a third straight defeat; Burleson went hitless, though his hundred eleven driven in still lead the National's ledger.

FIVE WALKS COME HOME TO ROOST IN A THREE-RUN SIXTH — HOLMES UNRAVELS AT CINCINNATI, AND THE BRUINS ARE PULLED BACK INTO THE DEAD HEAT: CINCINNATIS 6, BRUINS 4

Chicago led by a run behind Suzuki's two-run single and Happ's four-and-twentieth, but Clay Holmes walked five men through five and a third, and the sixth inning collected the arrears: Suárez singled the game level and Trevino lined a two-run knock for the lead, the freshly recalled Aguiar taking the decision and Pagán sealing his four-and-twentieth. The defeat, paired with Philadelphia's and San Diego's evening, closes the National's wild-card row into the three-way deadlock the October desk describes — the Bruins' cushion, a game and a half at Thursday's dawn, now vanished entirely.

A SIX-RUN FIFTH BOUNCES OFF THE MOUND AND INTO THE WESTERN METAL BUILDING — ELEVEN WINS IN TWELVE FOR THE SAN DIEGO NINE: SAN DIEGO NINE 8, GULF STREAM NINE 2

The go-ahead blow was Dustin Harris' single that caromed off the mound itself, and the exclamation was Ty France's towering three-run homer off the Western Metal Building — the heart of a six-run fifth — before Merrill's six-and-twentieth arrived in the eighth with a kiss planted on the barrel of his bat. Pivetta gave five innings of one for the victory. Eleven wins in twelve have carried the San Diego nine dead level with the Cubs and Phillies at the row's head, five clear of Arizona, with a clinch possible as soon as tomorrow; the Gulf Stream nine took their ten hits home for consolation.

FIVE IN THE FIRST WITHOUT THE CAPTAIN, AND COLE PASSES EVERY FIRST PICK BEFORE HIM — THE BRONX BOMBERS GAIN A GAME ON TAMPA BAY: BRONX BOMBERS 9, SNAKES 2

Hours after the calf verdict the ward above records, New York answered in the oldest dialect it knows: five runs in the first off Rodriguez, the fifteen-game winner, with Ben Rice walking one home before adding his team-leading nine-and-thirtieth homer and a triple, and the young George Lombard Jr. driving in three. Gerrit Cole gave six innings of two for the one hundred two-and-sixtieth victory of his career — passing Mike Moore for the most ever gathered by a first-overall draft selection — and the Bombers, winners of eleven in fifteen, drew within four of Tampa Bay before Tuesday's four-game reckoning. Carroll's two-and-twentieth was the whole of Arizona's answer; a third straight defeat leaves the Snakes five from the last chair with eight to play.

FIFTEEN HITS GO FOR NOTHING IN THE MOUNTAIN AIR — MONTES' NINTH-INNING THUNDER STEALS IT FOR THE PUGET SOUND MEN: PUGET SOUND MEN 5, MILE HIGH NINE 4

Seattle's early three — Crawford's homer on the game's first swing of consequence and Naylor's two-run single — were run down by degrees, McCarthy tripling and singling twice among Colorado's fifteen hits, and the Mile High nine led by the sixth. But Canzone's sacrifice fly squared it in the seventh, and in the ninth Lazaro Montes struck his fourth homer for the lead, Muñoz sealing the eight-and-twentieth save. It is a ninety-eighth defeat for Denver's men against a lone victory in their last ten — the arithmetic of a season now measured chiefly in patience.

SEVEN SPOTLESS INNINGS FROM PRIELIPP AND THE BOY JENKINS THUNDERS AGAIN — A WHITEWASH AT ANAHEIM: TWINS 3, ANGELS 0

Connor Prielipp gave the finest account of the evening's pitchers — seven scoreless innings, two hits, eight strikeouts — and Minnesota's three arrived by sacrifice fly, Bell's single, and Walker Jenkins' third home run, the youngster's second thunder in as many nights at the same address, his ninth-inning blow of Thursday having been entered in yesterday's card. Adams closed the four-hitter for his third save. The Angels, blanked, have now dropped five-and-ninety games; the same clubs resume this evening.

TWENTY YEARS TO THE NIGHT OF THE '4+1,' FOUR HOMERS IN A SINGLE INNING — BETTS STRIKES TWICE AND THE BOYS IN BLUE ROUT THE ORANGE AND BLACK: BOYS IN BLUE 8, ORANGE AND BLACK 2

Friday marked twenty years to the day since the '4+1' game of 2006, when four consecutive ninth-inning homers and Garciaparra's tenth-inning blow beat San Diego — and the champions honored the anniversary in kind, striking four home runs in the eighth inning alone: Muncy, Tucker, Mookie Betts with his second of the night, and Smith, in an evening begun with Betts' first-inning blow. Tyler Glasnow fanned ten across six innings for the victory, Díaz closed it in the return the convalescent desk sings, and all of it came without Ohtani. Lee's tenth homer and Cox's single made San Francisco's account, its shelved Webb entered in the ward above; the Boys in Blue hold four clear of Atlanta for the National's second seed, two behind Milwaukee.

The Saturday tables, then — with Atlanta's ticket punched and the captain of the Yankees on the shelf. In the American: clinched Tampa Bay holds the East by four over clinched New York, Boston nine and a half astern; the Central is Cleveland's by one over Chicago, the tiebreaker still Chicago's, as the lead columns relate; and the West is a dead heat at last, Houston and Texas level at seven-and-seventy wins and losses apiece, the Silver Boot tiebreaker in Houston's keeping. The wild-card row: New York and Boston seated in comfort, the last chair Chicago's by one over Texas, with Toronto two back and Baltimore three. In the National: Atlanta, berth in pocket, leads Philadelphia by five; crowned Milwaukee by eleven over Chicago; the crowned champions by nine over San Diego. And the wild-card ledger is the morning's marvel: Cubs, Phillies, and Padres level to the game at five-and-eighty wins and nine-and-sixty defeats — three clubs, three chairs, the order a matter of tiebreakers alone, San Diego seated third — with Arizona five back and eight to play. Today's bill is the full board of fifteen, verified against the schedule, and the desk commends: at 2:10 daylight baseball on the South Side, where Detroit and Chicago resume their argument, Jobe opposing Burke; at 4:10 Boston tries for the formal seating at Tampa Bay, where a berth may be sealed by evening, other scoreboards consenting; at 7:05 Soriano carries Toronto's thinning case against Quantrill at Arlington; at 8:10 Schlittler — fourteen victories and the American's best earned-run figure at 1.95 — takes the Yankee cause into Phoenix without the captain; and at 9:10 Skubal opposes the Orange and Black at Chavez Ravine. Eight mornings remain to the season's final page on the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~
