entry.title: EIGHTEEN PITCHES, TWELVE OF THEM BEATEN FOUL — A ROOKIE'S WALK CRACKS THE SUMMIT OPEN, AND A SIX-RUN SIXTH GIVES CHICAGO THE SERIES THAT MAY DECIDE THE CENTRAL: WHITE SOX 7, GUARDIANS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 69 · Tuesday, the Fifteenth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 10 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

EIGHTEEN PITCHES, TWELVE OF THEM BEATEN FOUL — A ROOKIE'S WALK CRACKS THE SUMMIT OPEN, AND A SIX-RUN SIXTH GIVES CHICAGO THE SERIES THAT MAY DECIDE THE CENTRAL: WHITE SOX 7, GUARDIANS 3

The fixture of the week delivers its opening argument: Peters outlasts Williams in the longest plate appearance of the major-league season, Teel and Vargas cash the runs behind him, and the White Sox leave Cleveland's own park holding a game-and-a-half lead and the tiebreaker besides

Eighteen pitches. Twelve of them, with two strikes on him, beaten foul by a rookie outfielder who fell behind no-balls-and-two before the sixth inning at Cleveland was a minute old. Tristan Peters against Gavin Williams — the August Rookie of the Month against the big right-hander Cleveland had held back a full week precisely for this series — became, by the count of the bureau's machines, the longest plate appearance in the major leagues this season, tied for the fifth-longest since such things were first written down in 1988, and the equal of Adam Kennedy's 2004 mark for the most pitches ever thrown in a walk. For that is how it ended: ball four, Williams' evening done at a season-high one hundred thirteen pitches, and the floodgates propped open behind him. "It felt like I was up there for like an hour," Peters deposed afterward. "I was exhausted." His opposite number could only tip the cap: "I counted at one point, and I just stopped counting because it was getting up there." The Cleveland manager Vogt, whose club lost the game on the exchange, called it "two very good players going at it — entertaining to say the least," which is a gracious way to describe a mugging.

What followed was the six-run sixth that settled the fixture this desk has called the week's own for three mornings running. Williams had carried a shutout through five despite a bases-loaded escape in the fourth; the relief that inherited his mess found no such fortune. Andrew Benintendi sprinted home when the first baseman Lowe's throw struck Peters on the back of the head — the young man praised by his manager Venable for "getting into the throwing lane," a spring-training fundamental executed at the season's loudest hour — and then the honest artillery: Kyle Teel doubled two across with the bases full, and Miguel Vargas struck a two-run homer, his one-and-thirtieth, a measured two-and-ninety feet past three hundred to left. Six runs in the frame, every one of them chargeable to the ledger of a single walk. The opener Newcomb and the bulk man Sean Burke — five innings, one unearned run, the decision to nine-and-seven — kept the hosts quiet until garbage time, Fry's two-run homer in the ninth the whole of Cleveland's late reply. "It's no secret what's on the line here, so to win the first game is huge," said Burke. "To play in a game like this is a privilege."

The consequences are the sternest of the September. Chicago's hold on the Central widens to a game and a half, and — the connoisseur's item — the victory clinches the season's series between the two clubs, so that a dead heat at the wire now goes to the White Sox. Cleveland, which had rearranged its whole rotation to open this set strong, must now win the two games that remain in it merely to keep the argument alive; the visitors' young left fielder Martínez left the evening clutching a flank besides, as the ward below records. "It's just one game," Williams insisted. "You play 162 for a reason." True enough — but of the 162, the Herald submits, some weigh more than others, and last night's weighed a game and a half plus a tiebreaker. Game two goes at 6:40 this evening, Martin opposing Griffin and his fifteen victories.

News Around the League

THE CLINCHING DESK: TWO MORE TICKETS PUNCHED IN A SINGLE EVENING — THE CHAMPIONS' FOURTEENTH OCTOBER RUNNING TIES THE OLDEST STREAK IN THE BOOKS, AND THE YANKEES' BERTH ARRIVES BY WIRE FROM TORONTO

The postseason's ledger of the admitted doubled itself last night. In Cincinnati the champions dispatched the Reds four-to-one — the particulars stand in the card below — and thereby entered their fourteenth consecutive postseason, drawing level with Atlanta's 1991-to-2005 run for the longest such streak the game has ever kept. The celebration was a handshake line, nothing more; champagne is not uncorked in that clubhouse for formalities. "We don't take it for granted," said Max Muncy, the longest-tenured of them, "but it is the expectation here." The expectations beyond: a thirteenth West flag in fourteen years, held by nine games over San Diego with the tiebreaker banked; a first-round bye, three and a half clear of Atlanta for the second seed; and the game's first three-peat since the Yankees of 1998 to 2000.

Which brings the desk to those Yankees' heirs, whose own ticket arrived by the strangest of couriers. New York beat Minnesota eight-to-three, as the card tells, but the berth itself was sealed in Toronto, where the Blue Jays' ninth-inning stumble against Detroit did the arithmetic for them — a third consecutive October for the Bronx, and the eighth in the manager Boone's nine years. "We've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Boone allowed amid the clubhouse noise. "Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group." The pitcher Warren put the house's ambition more plainly: "This is the baseline. This is what we're expected to do." Four clubs now hold October's paper — Tampa Bay, Milwaukee, Los Angeles, New York — and the reader will note the season's first two admissions came by walk-off thunderbolt and twenty-run carnival, the latest two by handshake and by telegram. September distributes its drama unevenly.

THE LAUREL DESK: THE FINAL CY YOUNG CANVASS IS UNANIMOUS TWICE OVER — SCHLITTLER AND MISIOROWSKI, EACH AT 1.95, SLAM THE DOOR ON BOTH LEAGUES AT ONCE

Only yesterday these columns recorded the Bronx chatter drifting from Cy Young toward Most Valuable; this morning the wires certify that the first conversation, at least, is over. MLB.com's final poll of the season — two-and-thirty voters, ranking five deep — returned Cam Schlittler of the Yankees and Jacob Misiorowski of the Brewers as unanimous first choices in their leagues, every first-place vote to both men. The symmetry is the connoisseur's delight: each leads his league with an earned-run figure of precisely 1.95, tied for the lowest among all qualified pitchers in the game. Schlittler has allowed one run or fewer in each of his last seven starts; Misiorowski's two hundred six-and-thirty strikeouts are tied for the major-league lead — with Toronto's Cease, the American's runner-up, whose own two hundred six-and-thirty are a personal high and whose .177 average against is the league's stingiest. The rest of the American's ballot ran Messick, Rasmussen, Gray; the Herald notes with approval that an award poll and a pennant race have rarely shared so many principals. Misiorowski, as it happens, takes the hill this very evening at Pittsburgh — on Roberto Clemente Day, in the great man's own park, as the almanac below explains. The voters may be finished; the season is not.

THE MILESTONE DESK: FLUSHING CHEERS ITS POLAR BEAR IN VISITING ORANGE — ALONSO'S HOMECOMING FINDS HIM ONE BLOW SHY OF THREE HUNDRED

Pete Alonso walked to the visitors' end of a long and familiar hallway at Citi Field last night, dressed for the first time in his life to play against the Mets — and the house that watched him hit two hundred four-and-sixty home runs in its colors, more than any Met who ever lived, declined to treat him as a visitor. They chanted his name at batting practice, chanted it again after the anthem, and rose for a tribute reel before the first pitch; the man tipped his cap to the thunder. "Honestly, it's a little weird," he confessed. "I lived a lot of life here... It's much appreciated." The evening's line was a quiet nought-for-three with a walk, but the ledger around it is anything but quiet: those two hundred four-and-sixty homers as a Met plus the five-and-thirty of this Baltimore summer leave him at two hundred nine-and-ninety for his life — one swing from the three-hundred club — with his hundred runs driven leading all the American besides. The wires note his favorite memory of the old place remains the winning blow he struck against Milwaukee in the Wild Card round of 2024. The new place got the winning blow last night from another hand entirely, as the card below sings, and the Herald suspects Flushing will cheer rather less if number three hundred arrives before the set concludes.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: MIAMI FOLDS MEYER'S TENT FOR THE YEAR, ATLANTA'S LÓPEZ JOINS THE SHELF WITH ELEVEN TO PLAY, AND CLEVELAND HOLDS ITS BREATH OVER A FLANK

The gravest entry is Miami's. Max Meyer, an All-Star in the season's first half — the Marlins' first starter so honored since Alcantara in 2022 — has thrown his last pitch of 2026: the club halted his throwing program and shut him down, the neck strain that has shelved him since July refusing to yield. "He just wasn't able to get past the hump," said the manager McCullough, who chose a sound offseason over a longshot September. The man leaves behind one hundred eleven innings, far his most, and a sweeper the measuring machines rank among the game's best; the ward wishes the arm a quiet winter.

Atlanta's file thickens at the worst hour. Reynaldo López, chased in the third inning at Wrigley as the card below records, goes to the fifteen-day invalid list with discomfort of the right shoulder — "we've got to change course here," said the manager Weiss — and the East leaders, four and a half up with eleven to play, are down to Sale, Mahle, Holmes, and Pérez among starters who figure in October. The rookie Ritchie comes up from Gwinnett for tomorrow's turn, and Smith-Shawver's five innings of relief last night read like an audition for the playoff bullpen. In Cleveland, meanwhile, the young outfielder Angel Martínez winced through a seventh-inning swing and left the summit's opener with inflammation of the right flank — "we pulled Angel out of precaution," said Vogt; "we'll know more tomorrow" — words no club cares to speak with the division on the table. The lesser entries: Toronto's Rudy Martin Jr. to the ten-day list with a hamstring, and the champions' reliever Henriquez shelved with a barking lower back, the once-heralded Bobby Miller recalled to fill the room. The candle burns for all.

THE ALMANAC DESK: THE ONE-AND-TWENTY FLIES ON EVERY BREAST TODAY — ROBERTO CLEMENTE DAY ARRIVES, AS THESE COLUMNS HAVE TWICE PROMISED

Twice this week the almanac has pointed the reader to the fifteenth of September; it is here. Across all thirty parks today the game honors Roberto Clemente — fifteen times an All-Star, three thousand hits exactly, and a man who died on New Year's Eve of 1972 flying relief to earthquake-stricken Nicaragua — with a No. 21 patch on every jersey in the major leagues. At Pittsburgh, where he played the whole of his eighteen years, every Pirate, coach, and manager wears the number entire for tonight's set with Milwaukee; nominees for the Clemente Award, past winners, and players of Puerto Rican blood may do likewise wherever they stand. The year's nominees, one to a club, make a roll the Herald is pleased to print in part: Arizona's Carroll, who as the card below attests spent last midnight authoring a walk-off; Detroit's ancient Verlander, whose homecoming these pages have kept in pencil; Kansas City's Witt; the Mets' Lindor; and Baltimore's Alonso, nominated in his first autumn away from Flushing. The day opens Hispanic Heritage Month across the game. The award itself — for character, for the community, for the game carried beyond the foul lines — is the only laurel in the sport named for what a man does when no box score is kept, and the Herald holds it the equal of any column it prints.

The Rest of the Card

SEVEN SPOTLESS INNINGS FROM THE DEADLINE PRIZE, AND THE TICKET IS TAKEN WITH A HANDSHAKE — TUCKER AND HERNÁNDEZ SUPPLY THE THUNDER: BOYS IN BLUE 4, REDS 1

The clinching evening itself was almost businesslike, which was rather the point. Skubal, the mid-summer prize, gave seven scoreless innings of three hits with nine strikeouts — among his finest work in the new livery — while Kyle Tucker opened the account with his fifteenth homer, a third in five games from a bat warming at the season's best hour, and Teoscar Hernández followed a Tucker walk with a two-run blow, his fourteenth. Kiké Hernández singled home the fourth; De La Cruz's seven-and-twentieth homer off Phillips in the ninth spared Cincinnati the blanking. The fourteenth consecutive October thus secured — the full accounting stands in the clinching columns above — the champions permitted themselves a handshake line and turned to the next errand: Yamamoto opposes Lowder tonight in the set's second act.

A SIX-RUN EIGHTH IN A STEADY DRIZZLE, CROWNED BY THE GREAT MAN'S FIRST THUNDER SINCE THE INVALID LIST — JUDGE'S MOONSHOT FINDS THE SECOND DECK: PINSTRIPES 8, TWINS 3

The evening at Target Field was played in a drizzle and decided in a downpour. Trailing two-to-one into the eighth — Caballero's fourteenth homer the early account, answered when Emmanuel Rodriguez, the debutant these pages sang on Sunday, tripled home both Minnesota runs — New York stacked six in the frame: Caballero and Rice singled home three between them before Aaron Judge turned on a 2-2 cutter from Minter and deposited it in the second deck in left, a vintage moonshot measured at fifteen feet past four hundred. It was the great man's eighteenth homer and his first since returning from three months lost to a fractured rib. "The ultimate goal is to be ready for the postseason," he said afterward — a postseason whose ticket arrived mid-celebration by wire from Toronto, as the clinching columns record. Wells added his twelfth homer, Warren gave five and two-thirds without an earned run, and the pursuit of Tampa Bay holds at three and a half, with the four-game set in the Bronx on the twenty-second looming as the East's last argument.

THE WALK-OFF SWORD, SO LATELY MIAMI'S, TURNS IN THE HAND — CARROLL'S NINTH-INNING BOLT CAPS A RALLY FROM THREE DOWN: RATTLERS 8, GULF STREAM NINE 7

Two mornings ago these pages sang Miami's ninth-inning ambush of the champions; last midnight in the desert the same blade turned. The visitors led seven-to-four after seven honest innings — Sanoja a triple and a homer among three driven, Marsee a homer besides, and Burnes reached for five runs in under five frames — before Jordan Lawlar's two-run homer in the eighth drew Arizona within one. The ninth was cruelty by installments: the closer Fairbanks walked Moreno, threw a single pitch to Perdomo, and left the game hurt; the reliever Ralston inherited the bunt that moved the pinch-runner Troy to second; and Corbin Carroll, who confessed he had spent the pitching change planning the at-bat, got the hung splitter he was hunting and struck it for a two-run, walk-off homer, his one-and-twentieth. "One of those catalyst type of games that pushes you forward," ruled the manager Lovullo. The arithmetic: Arizona holds at two and a half behind streaking San Diego — three in the loss column — with the season's final weekend at Petco still fated for the two of them; a third straight defeat, and the spiral was on. The club also claimed the outfielder Jesús Sánchez off Toronto's waiver wire in the morning, stocking the bench for the stretch. Miami, which shut its All-Star Meyer down for the year as the ward reports, flies home with a hard week's lesson: the walk-off is a lender, and it always calls the loan.

SIX HITLESS INNINGS UNDONE IN A QUARTER HOUR, AND THE NIGHT ENDS ON A THROW THAT CLIPS THE CLOSER'S GLOVE — A FIFTH STRAIGHT FOR DETROIT: TIGERS 6, JAYS 5

Toronto was one out into the seventh inning of a no-hitter and, by the eighth, one mistake from October's exits. Soriano carried the no-hit bid six and a third before Detroit landed five hits around a single out — Dingler's run-scoring single, Max Clark's two-run double, Torkelson's double behind it — and a two-run lead became a four-to-two deficit in minutes. Okamoto's three-run answer, his three-and-thirtieth homer, briefly restored the house's roar; Callahan tied it in the eighth; and the ninth supplied the season in miniature: Guerrero ranged far to his right and threw true, but the ball clipped the covering closer Varland's glove and rolled away, McKinstry racing home with the winning run. "I thought Vlad made a good throw," said the manager Schneider. "We just didn't execute it." Kinley took the decision, Jansen sealed his twentieth save, and the schooling Tigers — winners of five running with the Verlander homecoming still penciled at the calendar's edge — play kingmaker with evident relish. For the Jays the ledger is grim reading: a game behind Cleveland's chair, holders of the tiebreaker over the Clevelands as this paper has noted — but one-and-five against Chicago, so the Central's own argument now bears directly on which club they must catch. The same clubs go again at 7:07 tonight.

FOUR HITS, THE HUNDREDTH RUN DRIVEN, A SEVEN-AND-THIRTIETH THEFT, AND A TWO-AND-FORTIETH HOMER TO STAND BESIDE SWEET-SWINGIN' BILLY: CUBS 7, TOMAHAWK NINE 3

Pete Crow-Armstrong gave Wrigley Field the full catalogue: a two-run double in the second that carried his runs driven to one hundred exactly, a single and his seven-and-thirtieth stolen base in the fourth — the forty-forty ledger, entered in these pages Saturday at four steals wanting, now wants but three — a two-run homer in the sixth, his two-and-fortieth, and a single in the eighth for good measure. The homer is the historian's item: it draws him level with Billy Williams' 1970 figure for the most in a season by any left-handed batter in all the Cubs' long annals. "It's great company to keep," ruled the manager Counsell; the young man, who counts the Hall of Famer a friend, allowed that this was one distinction "I'll buy into." Peterson — a Met, the reader will smile, when Chicago bought this very future in 2021 — held Atlanta to a run into the seventh; Yastrzemski's pinch two-run homer dressed the visitors' line late. The Braves' evening cost them double: López lasted but three innings and went to the invalid list by midnight, as the ward above tells, and the East's lead is pared to four and a half over Philadelphia. The Cubs, for their part, sit atop the National's wild-card row and welcome the same clubs back at 7:40 tonight.

ON THE NIGHT FLUSHING CHEERED ITS OLD HERO, THE ONLY THUNDER THAT COUNTED WAS BALTIMORE'S — HENDERSON'S EIGHTH-INNING BLAST KEEPS THE CANDLE LIT: ORIOLES 2, METS 1

The sentiment belonged to Alonso, as the milestone columns above attest; the decision belonged to Gunnar Henderson. With the account level at one in the eighth, the shortstop turned on a slider from Núñez and sent it seven-and-ninety feet past three hundred over the wall in right-center — his three-and-twentieth homer, his first since the thirtieth of August, and the end of a twelve-game drought of runs driven that had shadowed a difficult year. "I feel like I've been swinging at a lot of the right pitches," he said. "Glad I came through then." Kjerstad's run-scoring double had opened the evening's business; the rookie Tong gave the Flushing nine six fine innings around Ewing's tenth homer, and got nothing for them. Baltimore's Young walked five and stranded eight across five stubborn innings before four relievers closed the door, Garcia sealing it. Two straight now for the obstinate Orioles, three games from the American's last chair — and the wires observe that Henderson, at five-and-twenty, has a hit in eight of his last ten as he plays a hard season out with evident pride.

SIX RUNS BY THE THIRD, THEN A LONG EVENING OF WHITE KNUCKLES IN THE MOUNTAIN AIR — THE EIGHTH STRAIGHT MATCHES THE SEASON'S BEST: SAN DIEGO NINE 8, MOUNTAIN MEN 7

The surge this paper has chronicled through a full week reached eight consecutive victories by the now-customary method: a fortune banked early and defended with the fingernails. Machado opened with his eight-and-twentieth homer, the second inning produced four more — Tatis' two-run blow, his two-and-twentieth, the heaviest — and at six-to-one the evening looked a stroll. Coors Field permits no strolls: Colorado's fourteen hits kept arriving, McCarthy's two-run triple and Carrigg's homer among them, and the margin required Ty France — activated from the paternity list only that afternoon — to single home the seventh run with two out in the seventh, part of a three-hit return. "It's just the time of year where you've got to win," said the new father. "It doesn't matter how you do it." Miller sealed his seven-and-thirtieth save with the tying run aboard. The third wild-card chair stays San Diego's by two and a half over Arizona — three in the loss column, the figure that matters — while the Rockies absorb an eighth straight defeat, their five-and-ninetieth of a long year. The same clubs go again at 8:40 tonight.

TEN MEN UP, TEN MEN DOWN, AND NOT A HIT UNTIL THE SIXTH — THE ROOKIE MATHEWS DEALS, BERNAL STEERS, AND BURLESON REACHES ONE HUNDRED TEN: CARDINALS 2, GIANTS 1

St. Louis' September of auditions produced its finest recital yet. The rookie left-hander Quinn Mathews retired the first ten San Francisco batters, carried a no-hit bid into the sixth until McCray's double broke it, and finished with eight strikeouts across six and two-thirds innings of a single run — crediting his fellow rookie, the catcher Bernal, for the navigation: "I think I shook one pitch in three innings." Bernal steered and hit besides, three hits with a run driven in, while Burleson's run-scoring single carried his league-leading count to one hundred ten. The reliever Bruihl stranded the bases full in the seventh with the night's only batter faced, and O'Brien sealed his seven-and-thirtieth save. The Giants' whole account was Cox's single; a fourth consecutive defeat deepens the gloom of an outfit playing out the string without Devers, whose season, as yesterday's ward recorded, ended on a surgeon's calendar. The clubs meet again at 7:45 this evening.

A PERFECT RELAY SETS THE TONE AND DETMERS BANKS A SEVENTH STRAIGHT QUALITY START — ONE STRIKEOUT NOW FROM TWO HUNDRED: ANGELS 6, PUGET SOUND MEN 4

The first inning at Anaheim told the whole evening in miniature: Crawford aboard, Arozarena's double into the gap, and the relay — Siri to Neto, the shortstop's throw home registered at seven-and-ninety miles to the hour and a shade more — cutting the runner down at the plate. "That relay set the tone," ruled the manager Suzuki, and behind it Reid Detmers did what he has done all the season's second half: six innings, three runs — all on Raleigh's three-run homer — and eight strikeouts for a seventh consecutive quality start. Since the All-Star interval his earned-run figure stands at 1.65, the best in the major leagues, and his strikeout count rests at one hundred nine-and-ninety: one more makes him the first Angel to two hundred since Ohtani in 2022, and the first left-handed one since Finley in 1999. Neto — the club's Clemente nominee, the almanac notes — tripled home a run and scored twice, Siri collected three hits, and the rookie Guzman's two-run single supplied the cushion. Seattle's long season leaks another; the same clubs conclude at 9:38 tonight.

The Tuesday tables, then — with four flags of certification now flying. In the American: clinched Tampa Bay holds the East by three and a half over clinched New York, Boston eight and a half astern of the leaders; the Central is Chicago's by a game and a half over Cleveland with the season's tiebreaker banked besides, as the lead columns sing, and game two of the summit goes tonight; the West, where neither principal played, stands Houston by a single game over Texas. The wild-card row: New York and Boston seated in comfort, the last chair Cleveland's by one over Toronto — who hold the tiebreaker on the Clevelands but not on the White Sox, a distinction that may decide their October — with Texas a game and a half back and Baltimore three. In the National: Atlanta by four and a half over Philadelphia, its rotation thinning as the ward reports; clinched Milwaukee by nine and a half over Chicago; the clinched champions by nine over San Diego. The wild-card ledger: the Cubs at the row's head, Philadelphia a half-game behind them, San Diego in the third chair by two and a half over Arizona — three in the loss column — with Pittsburgh seven back and St. Louis seven and a half. The desk's Monday bill delivered in full: the summit to Chicago, the champions' clinch at Cincinnati, the Yankees' evening ended in a berth, and the desert matter settled by walk-off. Tonight's bill is the full board of fifteen, verified against the schedule, and the desk commends four engagements to the reader's lamp: at 6:40 the summit's second act in Cleveland, Martin opposing Griffin and his fifteen victories; at 6:40 the unanimous Misiorowski takes the hill at Pittsburgh on Clemente Day, every Pirate wearing the one-and-twenty; at 6:45 Sánchez, seventeen-and-five, carries Philadelphia into Washington; and at 7:07 Toronto, wounded twice over, tries Detroit again with the arithmetic tightening at its back. The almanac stands at attention today: Roberto Clemente Day across all the leagues, as the columns above record. Twelve mornings remain to the season's final page on the seven-and-twentieth, and the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

The Herald Acknowledges Its Debts

entry.title: TWO RUNS DOWN, THREE OUTS LEFT — AND A MAN OFF THE BENCH ENDS IT WITH ONE SWING: RAMÍREZ'S PINCH-HIT THUNDERBOLT CAPS A FOUR-RUN NINTH AGAINST THE CHAMPIONS, MARLINS 6, DODGERS 4
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 68 · Monday, the Fourteenth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TWO RUNS DOWN, THREE OUTS LEFT — AND A MAN OFF THE BENCH ENDS IT WITH ONE SWING: RAMÍREZ'S PINCH-HIT THUNDERBOLT CAPS A FOUR-RUN NINTH AGAINST THE CHAMPIONS, MARLINS 6, DODGERS 4

An infield scratch, a bunt laid down like a calling card, Sanoja's tying double, and then the walk-off blow into the left-center saloon — Miami's seventh walk-off of the summer takes the season's series from Los Angeles for the first time in five years

The ninth inning at Miami arrived wearing the champions' colors. Los Angeles led four runs to two, Mookie Betts having restored the margin in the top of the frame with a ground-rule double — this a day after his ten-thousandth-in-franchise-annals homer filled these columns — and the visitors stood three outs from salvaging the set's finale. What followed was a rally built of the game's smallest coins and its largest: Xavier Edwards beat out an infield scratch, Jakob Marsee laid a bunt down like a calling card, and Javier Sanoja lined a double into the left-field corner, his thirtieth, to bring both men home and square the account at four. The reliever Scott, charged with the mess, gave way to Stewart — and the manager McCullough reached down his bench for Agustín Ramírez, who had not started the day and finished it instead: a four-seam fastball at very nearly five-and-ninety miles to the hour deposited deep into the Budweiser saloon in left-center, two runs, the game, the series, and the loudest half-minute of the Miami summer. "It's been a tough year for me," the young catcher deposed, "and that moment was a really beautiful moment for me, and I was enjoying every second."

The evening's earlier chapters had belonged to the visitors' nursery. Josue De Paula — whose début in this very park these pages chronicled Friday — collected the first hit of his major-league life and made it a three-run homer, the whole of the champions' early lead in one swing. Miami's answer began quietly in the eighth, Otto Lopez lining a two-run single, before the ninth's full production; the decision went to Fulton, the loss to Scott, now one-and-six.

The consequences are worth setting down slowly. Miami takes the season's series from Los Angeles for the first time since 2021, has now beaten the champions two days running — the eight-game streak these pages watched all week was snapped only Saturday — and banks a seventh walk-off victory of the year, closing an otherwise grey homestand before boarding for nine games on the road, beginning this very evening in the desert. The champions, for their part, keep the West by nine over surging San Diego and open at Cincinnati tonight; but a club that stood three outs from taking the set and left with nothing will spend the flight counting the ones that got away.

News Around the League

THE INFIRMARY WARD: DEVERS' SEASON ENDS AT SEVEN-AND-THIRTY HOME RUNS — THE CORE THAT TROUBLED HIM FOR YEARS FINALLY COLLECTS ITS BILL, AND THE WARD'S ROUNDS RUN LONG

The gravest entry first. Rafael Devers, whose bat has carried San Francisco's autumn — eleven homers in his last eighteen games, seven-and-thirty in all, the most by a Giant since Bonds' five-and-forty of 2004, with eight-and-ninety runs driven besides — goes to the sixty-day invalid list with a core muscle injury he has played through most of the season, and his year is over. He travels to Philadelphia today to see Dr. Meyers, the same specialist who repaired his teammate Chapman's similar complaint last month, with surgery expected to follow. "I think it's something that's bothered him for a few years now and kind of something that was a mystery to him," said the manager Vitello, who noted the man had started 148 of the club's first 149 games and did not want to stop now. The Herald observes that the slugger fell one homer shy of his own career figure, and that a bid for the first forty-homer Giant season since Bonds dies on an operating table's doorstep — a cruel arithmetic for a man under contract to the Bay through 2033, whose consolation must be a whole winter to heal.

The rounds elsewhere: Philadelphia's Luzardo, whose shoulder has occupied this ward three mornings running, is now hoped by the interim manager Mattingly to pitch sometime next week — progress, measured in hope. Houston's Correa travels home for re-evaluation of the surgical ankle, a minor-league rehabilitative assignment ideally to follow within the week. In the Bronx, Schmidt could return from his elbow reconstruction during the Minnesota series that opens tonight. And the champions' ward stays crowded: Freeman rests the aching knee today, Rojas left yesterday's defeat clutching a shoulder, and Ohtani may resume swinging a bat as early as today by the manager Roberts' telling.

THE VALEDICTORY DESK: ONE LAST CLIMB UP THE COMERICA HILL — DETROIT AIMS ITS FAREWELL TO VERLANDER AT THE SEASON'S NEXT-TO-LAST DAY, IN PENCIL BUT IN EARNEST

The Tigers have already promised a Verlander Career Celebration for the regular season's final weekend; now they are trying to deliver the man himself to the hill for it. Justin Verlander, one-and-twenty seasons into the work, signed back to Detroit in February for precisely this homecoming and has been denied it all year — a hip, then a hamstring, his only outing of 2026 a March start in Arizona — but Saturday's mound session, fastballs reported at three-and-ninety miles to the hour, puts him on a schedule: bullpen work this week, a simulated game next weekend, and, if the body consents, a start on Saturday the six-and-twentieth, the season's next-to-last day. "In pencil, we're aiming for that last weekend," said the manager Hinch, careful as a man carrying china. "But we can't have a setback of any sort, and I don't want to make a false promise." The man himself owns the summer's disappointment plainly. The occasion wants no embroidery: Verlander has not pitched at Comerica Park in the home colors since August of 2017, eleven days before the trade that sent him to Houston and his championships. Nine years is a long walk home. The Herald will keep the date in pencil beside him.

THE LAUREL DESK: THE CHATTER AROUND SCHLITTLER TURNS FROM CY YOUNG TO MOST VALUABLE — EVERYONE IN THE BRONX SEEMS PERSUADED BUT THE MAN HIMSELF

Six more innings of one-hit pitching in yesterday's Subway finale — the full account stands in the card below — carried Cam Schlittler to the major leagues' best earned-run figure at 1.95, and carried the conversation around him somewhere grander. "I think valuable is a good word. He might be the MVP, too," ventured the manager Boone. "Just an awesome season, and hopefully there's a lot left in the tank." No pitcher has taken a Most Valuable Player award since Kershaw of the 2014 Dodgers, and the American's ballot is crowded with honest claimants — Houston's Alvarez, Tampa Bay's Caminero — but the fourteen victories, the eight-and-twenty strikeouts past two hundred, and the ERA lead make a case that will not be laughed out of the room. The dissent, charmingly, comes from inside the house: Judge, thrice the award's winner, allows that his teammate is "definitely pitching like an MVP" before noting that they keep a Cy Young Award for precisely this. The man himself declines the whole conversation and asks only for his next turn. The Herald's ledger observes merely that when the season's best pitching argument and its best pennant-race arithmetic wear the same uniform, October tends to settle these debates in person.

THE MILESTONE DESK: FISCHER MAKES IT EIGHT-AND-FORTY — THE BUSH-LEAGUE RECORD OF THE CENTURY GROWS BY ONE MORE, THIS ONE OFF A POSITION PLAYER'S LOB

The minor-league summer of Andrew Fischer, which this paper entered into its milestone columns Friday at seven-and-forty home runs, did not rest there. The Milwaukee prospect struck his eight-and-fortieth Saturday in Biloxi's nineteen-to-one carnival — this one, the wires confess, off a position player pressed into mound duty, the pitch ambling in at a stately seven-and-fifty miles to the hour — extending the largest homer harvest in a minor-league season this century. The connoisseur notes the finer print: eight-and-twenty of the blows have come since his promotion to Double-A, his September line stands at .353/.558/.882, and he leads every full-season bush-leaguer in slugging and OPS alike, with Kittle's fifty of 1982 the last figure left standing above him as the Biloxi schedule reached its final page. Whether the boy got another swing at history, this desk will report when the wires do; what is already banked is a first-round selection of 2025 outrunning every projection set against him, and a Milwaukee organization — its big club long since clinched, as these pages have sung — watching its future arrive ahead of schedule.

THE TRANSACTIONS DESK: ARIZONA PARTS WITH GURRIEL — AN ALL-STAR OF THE PENNANT AUTUMN OF '23, UNDONE AT LAST BY A LEDGER OF INJURIES

The Snakes designated Lourdes Gurriel Jr. for assignment yesterday, and the move reads like a short history of baseball's cruelty to the body. Three years ago the man was the marquee of Arizona's World Series October — an All-Star that summer, four-and-twenty homers, three more in the postseason — and signed a forty-two-million-dollar engagement to stay. Then September of 2025 took a knee ligament, this April a delayed début, a hamstring and an adductor took two more stints on the invalid list, and the sum of 2026 is one-and-fifty games at a career-worst .544 OPS with two home runs. He is two-and-thirty years old, and the club recalled the rookie infielder Fernandez from Reno to take the roster place. The Herald sets down the customary observation: the game's ledger forgets no one faster than a man it celebrated three autumns ago, and a veteran of his pedigree, once clear of the assignment wires, will find some contender curious about what remains in the barrel.

The Rest of the Card

NINETY WINS, FIRST IN ALL THE AMERICAN — AND A RECORD FIFTEENTH SWEEP, TAKEN FOURTEEN-TO-FOUR: GULF COAST CLUB 14, BAYOU CITY NINE 4

The clinched leaders spent Sunday setting figures in stone: the fourteen-run rout completed a weekend sweep of the West-leading Astros — the franchise's fifteenth sweep of the season, a club record and the major leagues' most — and made Tampa Bay the American's first ninety-win club, one-and-thirty games above the waterline. Aranda homered twice, his one-and-twentieth, among three driven; Palacios and Fortes added homers, Mesa Jr. a triple, and the decision went to Peralta. Houston's consolations were Paredes' one-and-twentieth and the return of the great Alvarez to the order after two days of the ankle parlor — a walk in two trips, his .310 still atop the batting race over the sprinter Simpson's .305. The sweep leaves the Astros thrice beaten running, their hold on the West pared to a single game over Texas, while the hosts hold the East by four over New York with thirteen to play.

SIX INNINGS, ONE HIT, AND THE SUBWAY RUBBER TAKEN COLD — SCHLITTLER'S 1.95 NOW LEADS BOTH LEAGUES: BRONX BOMBERS 2, METROPOLITANS 0

The rubber game these pages commended to the reader's lamp went precisely as the arithmetic suggested: Schlittler threw six innings of one-hit shutout pitching, his fourteenth victory, and the earned-run figure settled at 1.95 — the best in the major leagues, and the fuel for the awards chatter recorded in the laurel columns above. The runs were solo work: Rice's eight-and-thirtieth homer, which draws him level with Alvarez two behind Caminero's forty in the American's race, and Wells' eleventh; Bednar sealed it, his four-and-thirtieth. The Bombers thus take the Subway set two games to one and hold their pursuit of Tampa Bay at four, with the first wild-card chair theirs by a wide street; the Metropolitans, whose week of spoiling was genuine while it lasted, open with Baltimore tonight.

THREE HOME RUNS ON THREE CONSECUTIVE SWINGS OF THE ORDER — AND THE ONE IN THE MIDDLE IS VLADDY'S FIRST AT HOME ALL YEAR: MAPLE LEAF NINE 8, ORIOLES 1

The fifth inning at Toronto produced a thing the club had not done in fourteen years: Springer, Guerrero, and Okamoto struck home runs back-to-back-to-back, and the middle blow carried the afternoon's whole story. It was Guerrero's first home run at Rogers Centre in all of 2026 — the 289th plate appearance and hundred-and-fiftieth game of his waiting — struck off Rogers in the fifth, and the man stood at the plate and watched it go. "I know my stadium," he said afterward. "I know when I can stand at the plate." Okamoto's was his two-and-thirtieth, Springer's his fifteenth, and Cease — whose 2.38 these pages sent to the hill with the arithmetic yesterday — took the decision to eleven victories. The consequences: the Jays remain a single game behind Cleveland for the American's last chair, and hold the season's series between them, so a dead heat at the wire goes Toronto's way; Baltimore drifts three behind the Jays and further from the light.

BIBEE'S BOUNCE-BACK AND THREE HOMERS BESIDES, ON THE EVE OF THE SUMMIT — THE CENTRAL'S GAP IS DOWN TO HALF A GAME: FOREST CITY NINE 9, MINNESOTANS 2

Cleveland arranged its affairs precisely as a club would wish on the eve of the fixture of the week: Bibee struck out seven in the bounce-back start the wires had waited on, and the order supplied thunder in triplicate — Kwan's third, Bazzana's twelfth, Adell's one-and-twentieth — while Minnesota's answer was Larnach's thirteenth and little else. Paired with Chicago's stumble in St. Louis below, the arithmetic tightens to its final turn: the Central is now the South Siders' by a half-game only, and the two principals meet in Cleveland from tonight, the division to be argued in person at last. The Minnesotans, whose Saturday belonged to the debutant Rodriguez as these pages sang, greet the Yankees tonight.

THE LEAD SHRINKS TO A HALF-GAME AT THE WORST POSSIBLE HOUR — McGREEVY AND THE GAS HOUSE BULLPEN QUIET CHICAGO ON THE EVE OF CLEVELAND: GAS HOUSE NINE 3, SOUTH SIDERS 1

Whatever momentum Saturday's ninth-inning heroics bought the South Siders, Sunday spent it: McGreevy handled them to his seventh victory, Soriano sealed his fourth, and the three runs of St. Louis were ample against an order held to a single tally. The defeat, set beside Cleveland's rout above, cuts Chicago's hold on the Central to a half-game — the thinnest it has stood all month — on the very eve of the head-to-head set at Cleveland that this desk called the fixture of the week. Three of the last ten now for the Chicagos, who must rediscover their September on the road; the Gas House men, for their part, quietly bank a second straight and greet San Francisco tonight.

THE SINGLE SCALP IS TAKEN, AND HANDSOMELY — PAINTER GRINDS THROUGH THE GEORGIA HEAT, THE BATS DO THE REST, AND THE WILD-CARD SUMMIT IS SHARED: PHILADELPHIAS 9, BRAVES 4

Philadelphia left Atlanta with exactly the one victory this desk said they needed, and it was built the honest way. The rookie Painter wrestled the heat and his own command — one run allowed across a bases-loaded escape in the fourth, Acuña struck out with a fastball at seven-and-ninety in the first — and departed ahead; the order then buried the hosts, Realmuto's eleventh homer among nine runs, with Olson's nine-and-thirtieth the Braves' lone thunder and the decision falling to Alvarado. The ledger reads: the Philadelphias draw level with the Cubs atop the National's wild-card row, five behind Atlanta in the East with twelve to play, and open at Washington tomorrow with their ace's shoulder still in the ward's file above.

THE PROMISED ACE LASTS THREE INNINGS AND CINCINNATI WINS ANYWAY — THE SKID STOPS AT FIVE AGAINST THE LEAGUE'S BEST CLUB: CINCINNATIS 4, MILWAUKEES 3

Yesterday this desk sent Burns and his fifteen victories to Milwaukee carrying Cincinnati's pride; the ace lasted but three innings of two runs, and the pride arrived anyway. Suárez struck his four-and-twentieth homer, the bullpen — Williamson for the decision, Pagán for his three-and-twentieth seal — carried the remainder, and the Redlegs' five-game famine, entered in these pages with sympathy, is ended against the club least likely to permit it. Milwaukee's answer, Bauers' six-and-twentieth and Ortiz's ninth, fell a run short; the clinched Milwaukees, three-and-thirty runs across the set's first two evenings, took the finale philosophically at three-and-ninety wins, still the best figure in either league. The champions of the West arrive in Cincinnati tonight; the Milwaukees cross to Pittsburgh tomorrow.

TWO FROM THE BENCH AND ELEVEN HITLESS OUTS FROM THE BULLPEN — THE CORSAIRS AVOID THE SWEEP AND KEEP THE CANDLE LIT: CORSAIRS 4, BRUINS 3

The bill promised Chandler opposing Boyd, and Chandler collected: eight victories now, with Brandon Lowe sent up from the bench to drive two across and the Pittsburgh bullpen throwing three-and-two-thirds hitless innings behind him — a day after the same unit faltered, the wires note, which is the bullpen's way. Montgomery sealed his thirteenth; Amaya's sixth homer was the Bruins' best argument. The arithmetic stays stern for the Smoky City men — level at five-and-seventy wins and losses, six and a half from the National's last chair with twelve to play — but "there's still a chance," Lowe insists, "we're still playing meaningful games. That's all you can ask for right now." The Bruins, for their part, share the wild-card summit with Philadelphia still, and greet Atlanta at home tonight.

NINE PITCHES, NINE STRIKES, THREE MEN DOWN — TOLLE OPENS WITH AN IMMACULATE INNING AFTER THE RAIN, AND THE SERIES IS BOSTON'S: FENWAY MEN 4, ROYAL BLUES 1

The rain pushed the first pitch to nearly five o'clock, and Payton Tolle spent the waiting well: nine pitches, nine strikes, three strikeouts — an immaculate first inning, but the eighth such frame in all the Red Sox annals — and a fist pumped on the walk off the mound. "I don't think I had seen one in person," admitted the interim manager Tracy. "I have now." The runs came patiently thereafter, Roman Anthony's go-ahead single the hinge and Durbin's thirteenth homer the ornament; Whitlock took the decision in relief, Chapman sealed his four-and-thirtieth, and the veteran Kimbrel absorbed the loss. Boston thus banks the series, holds the second wild-card chair by six clear games, and carries a three-game winning run to Texas for tomorrow's opener.

BUTLER STRIKES TWICE, THE SECOND TIME WITH THE GAME IN HIS POCKET — A SECOND WALK-OFF OF THE SET FOR THE MACKMEN: MACKMEN 8, SEATTLE NINE 7

The West Sacramento set ended as it began, with Seattle walking off the field mid-celebration that was not theirs. Down four runs by the fifth, the Mackmen leveled with four in the seventh — Langeliers' two-run single the heart of it — and after Seattle nosed ahead again, Lawrence Butler ended matters in the ninth: his second homer of the day, a two-run bolt off the closer Muñoz, his sixteenth of the season. It answers Friday's tenth-inning walk-off and Saturday's nineteen-run Seattle reprisal, both chronicled in these pages — a series played entirely in exclamation points. Arozarena homered twice for the Seattle nine, his five-and-twentieth, in a beaten cause; Alvarado took the decision. The same two clubs part ways tonight, Seattle to Anaheim, the Athletics to Tampa Bay tomorrow to try their September mischief on the American's best.

SEAGER'S BLAST TRAVELS FOUR HUNDRED FIFTY-EIGHT FEET AND THE ROAD DROUGHT DIES WITH IT — QUANTRILL TAKES THE RUBBER MATCH FROM RODRIGUEZ: LONE STAR NINE 7, SNAKES 6

The desert rubber match this desk commended went to Texas, and by way of the season's longest Ranger home run: Seager's first-inning drive, measured at eight-and-fifty feet past four hundred, his eighteenth. Quantrill outlasted Rodriguez, now fifteen-and-six, and Latz sealed his nine-and-twentieth save with the tying run stranded at second — a shaky ninth survived, which is all a ninth must be. The victory ends a drought of genuine antiquity: eight consecutive road series lost since the start of July, the longest such run since 2021, now closed with the club's first road rubber game won since June. The arithmetic sharpens everywhere at once: the Lone Star nine sit one game behind reeling Houston in the West and two from the American's last chair, with Boston arriving tomorrow. The Snakes, Moreno and Arenado homering in the losing cause, fall two and a half behind San Diego and greet Miami's road show tonight.

FIVE RUNS OFF WEBB IN TWO INNINGS, A SEVENTH STRAIGHT, AND THE SWEEP — THE MISSION NINE NOW HOLD THE LAST CHAIR ALONE: MISSION NINE 6, ORANGE AND BLACK 4

The surge has its own momentum now. San Diego fell upon the Bay ace Webb for five runs inside two innings — Machado's seven-and-twentieth homer the heaviest blow — and then handed the evening to the bullpen, which has made a specialty of the late innings all week; the decision fell to the reliever Peralta, with Matsui sealing his first. Seven straight victories, a weekend sweep, and the National's third wild-card chair now held alone: two and a half clear of Arizona, a game and a half behind the Cubs and Philadelphias at the row's head. The Orange and Black, who learned only hours earlier that Devers' season was done — the ward above has the particulars — answered with Knizner's second homer and honest resistance, and their young hands drew the Padres manager's respect: "they're playing their tails off," Stammen allowed. The Mission nine ride the streak to Colorado tonight; the Giants call at St. Louis.

A FOURTH STRAIGHT FOR THE DETROITS AS THE SCHOOLING CONTINUES — GREENE REACHES TWENTY, TORKELSON THREE-AND-TWENTY, AND HUGHES FALLS TO NOUGHT-AND-EIGHT: DETROITS 8, MILE HIGH NINE 1

The matinee at Detroit ran to form and then some: Jobe took the decision, Greene struck his twentieth homer and Torkelson his three-and-twentieth, and the Detroits banked a fourth consecutive victory in a season whose truest business — the Verlander homecoming plotted in the valedictory columns above — waits at the calendar's far end. Colorado's whole account was Amador's fourth homer; the loss fell to Hughes, winless now in eight decisions, and the Mile High nine absorb a seventh straight defeat, their four-and-ninetieth of the year. Detroit crosses to Toronto tonight to play spoiler or kingmaker in the wild-card argument; the Coloradans host surging San Diego, which is nobody's idea of convalescence.

DOWN TWO IN THE EIGHTH, THE SENATORS ANSWER WITH FOUR — LILE'S TRIPLE TURNS THE AFTERNOON, AND THE CAPITAL RUN REACHES THREE STRAIGHT: SENATORS 6, HALOS 5

For the third day running the Capital club found the late chapter to its liking. Trailing four-to-two in the eighth — Ballesteros having struck a two-run homer and Neto his six-and-twentieth, with a twentieth stolen base besides, for the visitors — Washington strung four runs on honest carpentry: Lile's triple the turn of it, singles and Jacob Young's double completing the sum. The Halos clawed one back in the ninth and no more; the decision went to Tolman, with Sinclair sealing the first save of his career. Three straight now for the Senators, whose record-book pair Abrams and Wood — enrolled in the thirty-and-twenty brotherhood in Saturday's columns — keep finding themselves in the middle of victories. The Halos, losers of three running, greet Seattle at home tonight; Washington rests before Philadelphia arrives tomorrow.

The Monday tables, then. In the American: clinched Tampa Bay — first to ninety — holds the East by four over New York, Boston eight and a half astern; the Central is the argument of the hour, Chicago's by a half-game only over Cleveland, and the two clubs settle into Cleveland from tonight to argue it in person; Houston's hold on the West is down to a single game over Texas. The wild-card row: New York and Boston seated comfortably, the last chair Cleveland's by one over Toronto — who hold the season's series between them, the reader will note — with Texas two back. In the National: Atlanta by five over Philadelphia; clinched Milwaukee by ten over Chicago; Los Angeles by nine over San Diego. The wild-card ledger: the Cubs and Philadelphias share the head of the row, San Diego alone in the third chair by two and a half over Arizona, Pittsburgh six and a half back. The desk notes with quiet satisfaction that all five engagements it commended to Sunday's lamp delivered — the Subway rubber to Schlittler, the single scalp to Philadelphia, the chair-hungry afternoon to Cease, the desert rubber to Quantrill, and Cincinnati's pride upheld, though the promised ace needed his bullpen's charity. Tonight's bill is ten engagements, verified against the schedule, and the desk commends four: at 6:40 the Central's summit opens in Cleveland, Newcomb opposing Williams and his thirteen victories; at 6:40 also the champions call at Cincinnati, Skubal against Lodolo; at 7:40 the Yankees open in Minnesota, where the Bronx ward may yet return Schmidt to the colors; and at 9:40 Miami's road show opens in the desert, Alcantara opposing Burnes. The almanac reminds the reader that tomorrow, the fifteenth, is Roberto Clemente Day across the leagues; thirteen mornings remain to the season's final page on the seven-and-twentieth, and the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~
