entry.title: SIX HOME RUNS FALL UPON THE BRONX, AND TWO OF THEM ARE LINDOR'S — A LEADOFF BLOW AND A GRAND SLAM IN THE SAME AFTERNOON, A THING SEVEN MEN HAD DONE BEFORE HIM: METS 12, YANKEES 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 67 · Sunday, the Thirteenth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SIX HOME RUNS FALL UPON THE BRONX, AND TWO OF THEM ARE LINDOR'S — A LEADOFF BLOW AND A GRAND SLAM IN THE SAME AFTERNOON, A THING SEVEN MEN HAD DONE BEFORE HIM: METS 12, YANKEES 2

The soft-tossing rookie Thornton throws fire past the great Judge and prophesies his own double play, Cole is reached for three of the six, and the Subway rout before a sold-out house of 46,864 checks the Yankees' pursuit of clinched Tampa Bay at four games

The book on Zac Thornton runs to a single adjective — soft. He is by reputation among the gentlest-throwing pitchers in the major leagues, a man who lives on deception, seven pitches, and the edges of the plate. So when Aaron Judge stood in with two strikes in the first inning at Yankee Stadium yesterday afternoon, he could be forgiven for expecting a feather. What arrived instead was a fastball at ninety-five miles to the hour and a half beyond, on the inside corner, the equal of the hardest pitch the rookie has thrown all season; the great man watched it pass for strike three. An inning later Spencer Jones was frozen by its twin on the outside corner, and by day's end Thornton had thrown six such pitches at five-and-ninety or better across seven innings of two runs, one-and-eighty pitches the whole bill. "I didn't know the numbers of what was coming out of my hand," the young man deposed, "but I was getting good results, so I'm going to keep throwing it like that." His interim manager Green, surveying the fresh buzz cut atop the phenomenon, ventured that the barber deserved an assist.

The bombardment behind him was general. Francisco Lindor opened the contest with a leadoff home run off Gerrit Cole, and closed his afternoon in the eighth with a grand slam, five runs driven in all; the Elias bureau certifies him the eighth man in the game's long history to strike a leadoff homer and a slam in the same engagement. Between the bookends the visitors kept a steady artillery: Soto with his five-and-twentieth, Torrens with a homer and a double besides among three runs driven, Benge with his seventeenth, Jared Young with his ninth — six home runs in sum, three of them charged against Cole, whose line of four and one-third innings, nine hits, and five runs sends him to eight-and-nine and prolongs a September wrestle with the homer bug that the wires have begun to diagnose at length. The house of 46,864, sold to the rafters for the Subway matter, had little to cheer past Bellinger's fifteenth homer and a run-scoring single.

The curiosity of the day belongs to the seventh inning. Two Yankees aboard, one out, and Anthony Volpe — whose grand slam these pages sang two mornings ago — striding to the plate, the manager Green went to the mound himself for what he called a heat check. Thornton not only asked to remain; he predicted, in so many words, that he would coax an inning-ending double play. He then threw a changeup in a fastball count, and Volpe rolled it over, five-to-four-to-three, precisely as advertised. "Pretty impressive to call it like that," Green allowed afterward. The consequences read thus: New York's pursuit of clinched Tampa Bay is checked at four games, the first wild-card chair still theirs by four and a half over Boston, while the Flushing nine — ten games under the waterline yet winners of seven in their last ten — play the spoiler's part with evident appetite. The rubber game goes at 1:35 this afternoon, Scott opposing Schlittler and his league-leading 2.01.

News Around the League

THE MILESTONE DESK: TEN THOUSAND HOME RUNS SINCE THE FLIGHT WEST — BETTS SUPPLIES THE ROUND NUMBER AND MUNCY THE NEXT ONE, ON AN EVENING THE CHAMPIONS LOSE ANYWAY

The ten-thousandth home run struck by the Dodgers since the franchise removed from Brooklyn to Los Angeles in 1958 belongs to Mookie Betts. It came in the first inning at Miami with two out, an 85-mile splitter from Tyler Phillips that wandered to the middle of the plate and departed a measured nine-and-ninety feet past three hundred to left-center — Betts' twentieth of the season. "It's really cool," the great man said, confessing he had not known the round number was pending. "I didn't know that. So, I guess I'll always be remembered for something." Max Muncy followed at once with number ten thousand and one — his eight-and-twentieth of the summer, the two hundred forty-second of his life — and the champions led by two before the first inning was old.

That the evening thereafter went sideways, the streak of eight ending at the hands of the Floridians as the card below records, does not dim the ledger entry. Ten thousand home runs in the California annals alone, and the man who reached the figure is the same who this summer has made a habit of arriving at history's door as if by appointment.

THE RECORD BOOK: THE CAPITAL'S YOUNG PAIR SIGN A REGISTER OF ELEVEN — WOOD'S TWENTIETH THEFT SETS HIM BESIDE ABRAMS IN THE THIRTY-AND-TWENTY BROTHERHOOD

James Wood slid into the record books in the second inning at Nationals Park yesterday, his twentieth stolen base of the season joining his thirty home runs — and because CJ Abrams reached the same twin figures only last weekend, the two young Washingtonians become the eleventh pair of teammates in all the game's history to post thirty homers and twenty thefts in a single season. The register they sign is good company: Lindor and Soto did it for the Mets only last year — the same two men, the reader will smile to note, who spent yesterday afternoon dismantling the Yankees in the lead columns above — and the roll runs back through Griffey and Rodriguez, Beltrán and Wright, to Johnson and Strawberry of 1987. At five-and-twenty and three-and-twenty years respectively, Abrams and Wood are but the second such pair aged five-and-twenty or younger, standing beside Lindor and Ramírez of the 2018 Clevelands; no Washington man had managed a thirty-and-twenty season at all since Soriano's forty-and-forty of two decades past.

"They're both total-package players, and I'm lucky just to be able to sit there and watch them do their thing," said the manager Butera, whose pair credit the first-year first-base coach Corey Ray with the larceny curriculum. Wood, who missed seven-and-twenty games to a strained oblique and has stolen more bases regardless than in all of last season, states the next ambition plainly enough — one more homer ties his career figure, and the thirty-and-thirty club waits beyond. Abrams, for his part, did not stop at the milestone: his theft of third base in the tenth inning yesterday preceded the winning run by a matter of moments, as the card below tells. "That's what great players do," ruled Butera.

THE PRODIGY DESK: SUMMONED AT MORNING, IMMORTAL BY THE THIRD INNING — THE TWINS' RODRIGUEZ STRIKES A FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FOOT HOME RUN IN HIS FIRST MAJOR-LEAGUE AT-BAT

The season's nursery delivers again. Emmanuel Rodriguez, the fifth-ranked prospect of the Minnesota organization, was called up from St. Paul yesterday morning, written into the ninth place of the order in center field, and in the bottom of the third inning — his first at-bat as a major leaguer — hit a 2-1 fastball from the Cleveland right-hander Aleman a measured four hundred twenty feet for a home run, leveling a game his club would win by a run, as the card below attests. The blow was six years in the transit: injuries held the young man to three hundred three-and-fifty minor-league games across six professional seasons, and the organization's patience with his mending has been a standing item of the prospect wires. "After all these hard-working years and all the time it's taken, I still want to enjoy myself," he had said before the game, his teammate López interpreting. "It's going to be a big moment, but I just want to take the field, enjoy and do my baseball thing."

The Herald notes the calendar's generosity: this is the second début inside three mornings to arrive gift-wrapped, after the Dodgers' De Paula took his first at-bats in Miami on Friday evening as these pages then recorded. September rosters swell, and the game's future keeps introducing itself mid-pennant-race — the Herald holds the door and takes down the names.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: LUZARDO AWAITS THE VERDICT OF THE IMAGING MACHINES, AND THE BATTING RACE'S LEADER IS KEPT IN THE PARLOR BY AN ANKLE

The ward's gravest file thickens. Jesús Luzardo, whose scratching from Saturday's start in Atlanta these pages reported yesterday, underwent an examination by the imaging machines Friday evening on the aching left shoulder, and his next turn is now listed as to-be-determined — words no contender enjoys reading in September. The man himself preaches calm: "not concerned," runs his verdict, appended with a soldier's flourish — "If today was Game 7 of the World Series, I'm throwing, no matter what." The trouble dates from the days after Monday's two-hit blanking of these same Braves; Philadelphia, whose evening without him went as badly as an evening can, as the card below grimly attests, can spare neither the arm nor the time.

In the American, meanwhile, Yordan Alvarez sat a second consecutive game in St. Petersburg with a soreness of the right ankle, the souvenir of an awkward step upon third base Thursday evening — he waved off the trainers at the time, as strong men will. The absence ended a run of two-and-sixty consecutive starts, and the manager Espada holds hope for this afternoon's finale. The stakes want no restating: Alvarez still leads the American's batting race at .310 over the sprinter Simpson's .306 — the strangest title argument ever run, which this paper examined at length yesterday, and which resumes the moment he returns, the two principals sharing the Tropicana premises through today. The wires note besides that his August fade has cost him the other two crowns for the moment, Caminero having passed him in homers at forty and Alonso in runs driven — the Baltimore man reaching nine-and-ninety just last evening. The candle burns for shoulder and ankle alike.

THE TRANSACTIONS DESK: TAMPA BAY SUMMONS A MAN WHO THROWS AT ONE HUNDRED TWO — AND THE PRICE ONCE PAID FOR HIM DROVE IN FOUR RUNS ELSEWHERE THE SAME EVENING

The clinched Rays, appetite undiminished, added velocity of the first order to their bullpen yesterday: Brody Hopkins, their seventh-ranked prospect and first among the pitchers, comes up from Durham bearing a fastball that has touched one hundred two miles to the hour and the number eight-and-eighty on his back. The right-hander Cook was optioned to make the room, and Grove was designated for assignment. "It's big, big stuff," ruled the manager Cash, "and we'll see if we can just harness it as many times over the plate as possible" — the strike zone having been, by the club's own admission, the young man's one intermittent acquaintance.

The connoisseur of symmetries will note the provenance: Hopkins came from Seattle in the summer of 2024 as part of the price for Randy Arozarena — and on the very evening of his summons, Arozarena himself struck his three-and-twentieth homer and drove in four runs amid Seattle's nineteen-run carnival in West Sacramento, entered faithfully in the card below. Both ledgers, it appears, are still paying out.

The Rest of the Card

TWO OUT, TWO STRIKES, AND THE CLOSER AHEAD IN THE COUNT — GRICHUK'S NINTH-INNING THUNDERBOLT STEALS THE EVENING BACK, AND THE CENTRAL'S CHAIR WIDENS TO A GAME AND A HALF: PALE HOSE 6, REDBIRDS 5

Chicago's season, which spent Friday night looking over its shoulder, spent Saturday night celebrating on the Busch Stadium grass. The evening had turned against them in the eighth, Bernal's leadoff homer off Taylor putting St. Louis ahead by a run; in the ninth the Redbirds' closer O'Brien — co-holder of the National's saves lead at six-and-thirty — got ahead of Teel no-balls-and-two before walking him, the seventh free pass of the night issued to a lineup that was also struck thrice by pitches. Then, two out and two strikes on him, Randal Grichuk lifted a drive that carried just beyond the leap of the right fielder Scott, and the Pale Hose led six-to-five, and that was the whole of the argument. "He's a battler. Never count him out," deposed the catcher Teel. "Leader of this team. He's always the first one here. Doesn't surprise me." The manager Venable spread the credit wider — the clubhouse, he noted, runs partly on the veteran's vigilance.

The arithmetic is the sweeter part: with Cleveland beaten in Minnesota, the Central's chair is Chicago's by a game and a half, with the magic figure at twelve. And the schedule now supplies the theater September owes: tomorrow evening the Pale Hose call at Cleveland itself, first of two, the division to be argued in person. Murakami, for the record, drove in a run besides; Winn cashed two for the beaten hosts.

THE DEBUTANT'S THUNDER AND THREE QUIET RUNS BESIDE IT — THE TWIN CITIES NINE CLIP CLEVELAND'S PURSUIT BY A RUN: TWIN CITIES NINE 4, CLEVELANDS 3

The afternoon at Target Field belonged to a man four hours into his major-league life — Emmanuel Rodriguez's first-at-bat homer, sung at proper length in the prodigy columns above, leveled the account in the third — and thereafter to the quiet industry of Clemens, Lewis, and Caratini, who cashed the runs that made it stand. Cleveland's reply ran through Bazzana, whose single brought Adell across, but the visitors could not square it; the decision went to Prielipp, and the loss to Aleman, into the annals now as the man who threw the debutant's pitch. The defeat is costlier than a Saturday in September ought to be: the Clevelands fall a game and a half behind the Pale Hose in the Central — whom they host tomorrow, first of two, with the division on the table — and their grip on the American's last wild-card chair is thinned to a single game over surging Toronto. The clubs conclude at 2:10 this afternoon, Bibee taking the ball for the visitors.

KIRK DRIVES IN THREE AND THE CANADIANS ANSWER FRIDAY'S INSULT — THE LAST CHAIR NOW BUT A GAME AWAY: CANADIANS 7, BALTIMORES 3

Toronto, beaten by these same birds Friday evening, replied with a thoroughness that speaks of urgency: Alejandro Kirk singled home one run and homered home two more — three driven in all — while Guerrero doubled and scored twice, Bateman added his second homer of the young career, Giménez doubled a run across, and Clement's sacrifice fly completed the seven. Baltimore's account was written almost entirely by one hand: Pete Alonso's five-and-thirtieth homer, a two-run blow that carries his league-leading count of runs driven to nine-and-ninety — the century mark now one errand away — with the third run a gift of Okamoto's throwing arm, twice errant on the evening. Arrighetti took the decision over Bradish. The Canadians, winners now of six in their last ten, sit but a single game behind Cleveland for the American's last chair — and this afternoon they send Cease and his 2.40 to the hill against Rogers at 1:37, the mathematics finally worth the candle.

PALACIOS CASHES TWO, MADRIGAL ONE, AND THE SUNSHINE NINE TAKE A SECOND STRAIGHT BY A WHISKER — HOUSTON'S HOLD ON THE WEST THINS TO TWO: SUNSHINE NINE 3, HOUSTON NINE 2

The clinched hosts continue to play as though nothing were settled, which is precisely the point — the East's flag, four games their own over New York, remains the stated ambition. Richie Palacios lined a single that brought Mesa Jr. and the sprinter Simpson across together, Madrigal's sacrifice fly added the third, and the bullpen made the slender sum stand, Wells taking the decision over Lambert. Houston's runs were Paredes' twentieth homer and a Diaz single that cashed Altuve, and no more — a second consecutive one-run defeat at the Trop, with the great Alvarez watching from the parlor as the ward above explains. The consequence out west is stern: the Astros' chair is now two games from Texas's reach, the thinnest it has stood in weeks. The set concludes at 1:40 this afternoon, Wesneski opposing Peralta, with the batting race's two principals possibly sharing a lineup card again at last.

TATIS HOMERS AND TWICE STEALS, THE JINTS' FOUR HOMERS GO FOR NOTHING, AND THE SURGE BY THE BAY RUNS TO SIX STRAIGHT: PADS 7, JINTS 6

San Diego's September surge rolls on — six victories running now, the last chair of the National held by a game and a half — though the evening by the Bay asked everything of them. Tatis struck his one-and-twentieth homer and stole two bases besides, his season's count of thefts reaching four-and-thirty; Merrill added his five-and-twentieth; and Dustin Harris — a quiet difference-maker in these pages two mornings running — drove in three more. San Francisco answered with four home runs — Devers' seven-and-thirtieth chief among them, Gilbert, Whitcomb, and the rookie Cavanaugh supplying the others, the last man's first of his major-league life — and still came up a run light, King banking his eleventh victory over the reliever Perdomo. The nightcap of the league's day goes at 7:20 this evening, Pivetta opposing Webb, with Arizona's stumble below keeping the arithmetic friendly.

SKENES DEALS LIKE HIMSELF AND IT IS SPENT LATE — O'HEARN DRIVES IN ALL THREE, AND STILL THE CUBBIES COME BACK: CUBBIES 4, SMOKY CITY NINE 3

Pittsburgh got the version of Paul Skenes that terrifies the league — the wires pronounce it a return to ace form — and contrived to lose anyway, the late innings coming apart as late innings will. Ryan O'Hearn drove in every Pittsburgh run, his eighteenth homer among the freight, and the visitors carried the lead deep before Chicago's patient correction: Busch's nineteenth homer and Ramírez's sixth anchored the reply, the decision falling at the last to Rolison — nine victories now against a single defeat — while the loss went to the reliever Soto. The comeback keeps the Cubbies first in the National's wild-card row, ten adrift of clinched Milwaukee in the division but four-and-eighty wins strong; the Smoky City nine, twice beaten running, drift six and a half from the last chair. The set concludes at 2:20, Chandler opposing Boyd.

A THIRD STRAIGHT HELPING, THIS ONE BY TEN — ACUÑA AND HARRIS SUPPLY THE THUNDER, THE VISITORS SUPPLY THE ERRORS, AND THE EAST'S GAP RUNS TO SIX: ATLANTAS 12, QUAKERS 2

Whatever Philadelphia came to Atlanta to settle is being settled against them. The third defeat of the set was the least dignified: Acuña struck his seventeenth homer among two runs driven — his career-long habit of tormenting this particular opponent now the wires' running theme — while Harris homered and drove in three, Baldwin cashed two more, and the innings were salted with Philadelphia misplays, Bohm and Stott each charged with an error. Mahle took the decision; Raley absorbed the loss; Harper's eight-and-twentieth homer and Crawford's third were the visitors' whole dinner. The ledger this morning is as stern as it has read all summer: Atlanta by six, its magic figure at seven, and the Quakers — thrice beaten running, their ace in the imaging machines' waiting room as the ward reports — must win today's finale at 1:35 behind Painter against Holmes merely to leave Georgia with a single scalp.

THE DESERT ANSWERS FRIDAY'S NINE WITH SIX OF TEXAS'S OWN — LANGFORD HOMERS, DURAN CASHES TWO, AND THE WEST'S SECOND PLACE CREEPS WITHIN TWO: TEXAS NINE 6, DESERT NINE 2

Friday's nine-run humiliation was returned with interest inside four-and-twenty hours. Langford struck his seventeenth homer, Duran drove in two to reach eighty on the season, and Jung, Nimmo, and Díaz cashed one apiece as Texas handled Pfaadt roughly and handed Garcia the decision. The consequences run in two directions at once: the Texas nine, with Houston beaten at the Trop, draw within two games of the West's chair, while the Desert nine slip a game and a half behind San Diego for the National's last seat, their winners' business of Friday undone at a stroke. The rubber game goes at 4:10 this afternoon and is among the day's best bills: Quantrill against Rodriguez, whose fifteen victories and 2.55 sit in the National's first rank.

THE STREAK STOPS AT EIGHT ON THE NIGHT OF THE TEN-THOUSANDTH — PAULEY CASHES TWO, GIBSON OUTLASTS GLASNOW, AND THE FLORIDIANS BANK ANOTHER SCALP: FLORIDIANS 4, ANGELENOS 3

The champions' eight-game march, chronicled in these pages to the point of monotony, was halted by the club that specializes in puncturing its betters at home. Los Angeles took its two-run lead on the famous first-inning pair — Betts' ten-thousandth-in-franchise-annals homer and Muncy's immediate echo, both certified in the milestone columns above — and thereafter went quiet, while Miami assembled its four with the lunch-pail: Pauley homered and drove in two, Lopez and Sanoja cashed one apiece, and the bullpen held the door. The defeat is charged to Glasnow, his first of the season against four victories, with Gibson taking the decision; the West's arithmetic is unmoved in substance, Los Angeles by ten with the flag figure at five. The set concludes at 1:40, Sheehan opposing Pérez.

THREE-AND-THIRTY RUNS IN TWO EVENINGS — MITCHELL DRIVES IN FOUR MORE, TURANG REACHES TWO-AND-NINETY, AND THE CREAM CITY MACHINE ROLLS A FIFTH STRAIGHT: CREAM CITY NINE 13, REDLEGS 9

A night after the twenty-and-nothing clinching carnival, Milwaukee scored thirteen more — three-and-thirty runs across two evenings against the same opponent, who may be forgiven for checking the schedule's exits. Garrett Mitchell, whose grand slam crowned Friday's rout, homered again and drove in four; Turang struck his nineteenth with two more runs driven, his season's count reaching two-and-ninety; Contreras added his seventeenth and three driven; and Patrick took the decision in the loose-jointed affair. Cincinnati's nine runs — Suárez's three-and-twentieth homer, three driven by the rookie Brito, De La Cruz cashing another — bought nothing but arithmetic: the Redlegs have now dropped five running. The finale at 2:10 brings the set's one genuine terror for the hosts: Burns, fifteen-and-three with a 2.73, takes the hill for the visitors against Gasser — though at three-and-ninety wins, the best record in either league, Milwaukee may receive even aces philosophically.

NINETEEN RUNS AND FIVE HOME RUNS — YOUNG DRIVES IN FIVE, AROZARENA FOUR, AND FRIDAY'S TENTH-INNING INDIGNITY IS AVENGED AT COMPOUND INTEREST: MARINERS 19, ATHLETICS 1

Walked off in the tenth on Friday, Seattle returned to West Sacramento and emptied the arsenal. Five home runs — Crawford's eleventh, Arozarena's three-and-twentieth, Canzone's two-and-twentieth, Cole Young's seventeenth, and the first of Arroyo's season — anchored a nineteen-run procession in which Young drove five across, Arozarena four, Arroyo three, and nearly every man in the order took a portion. Woo carried the decision to twelve-and-nine and was, remarkably, charged with the evening's untidiest moment, an error of his own making, there being nothing else to mark against the visitors' ledger. The Athletics' reply was a single run; their September mischief-making, seven victories in ten entering the night, absorbs its rudest interruption. The same clubs conclude at 4:05 this afternoon, Miller opposing Lopez.

SEVEN INNINGS, FIVE HITS, ONE RUN, NO WALKS — SUAREZ'S SECOND STRAIGHT GEM STOPS THE SKID AT THREE, AND ONLY THE BOY JENSEN ANSWERS: BOSTONS 5, MISSOURIANS 1

Boston's three-game stumble, entered with concern in yesterday's columns, was ended by the steadiest arm on the premises. Suarez gave seven innings of five hits and a single run, striking out eight and walking none — his second consecutive seven-inning gem, a run of form the man credits to a mechanical adjustment lately made — and the decision carries him to seven-and-four. Kansas City's whole reply was the work of Carter Jensen, the young catcher these pages saluted only yesterday, whose four-and-twentieth homer accounted for the run; Witt stole his fortieth base in the losing cause, drawing level with Chisholm one behind the sprinter Simpson's league-leading one-and-forty. The Bostons thus keep the second wild-card chair with a cushion of six clear games, and this afternoon at 3:05 send Tolle against Cameron for the set's conclusion.

ELEVEN RUNS AND A THIRD STRAIGHT FOR THE BENGALS — McGONIGLE STRIKES HIS SEVENTEENTH, LEE DRIVES IN THREE, AND GOODMAN'S EIGHT-AND-THIRTIETH IS WASTED ON THE MOUNTAIN AIR: BENGALS 11, COLORADANS 7

Detroit's autumn schooling of its young men produced its noisiest recitation yet: eleven runs, with McGonigle's seventeenth homer atop the pile, Lee driving in three, Keith stealing a base and cashing a run, and the supporting parts — Torres, Greene, Clark, Torkelson — each carrying freight in a third consecutive victory, Brieske taking his first decision of the year. Colorado's consolation was substantial where it was personal: Hunter Goodman struck his eight-and-thirtieth homer among three runs driven, a figure that lifts him into a share of the National's third place in that column, and Tovar added his eleventh. It bought no relief in the standings — the Coloradans have now dropped six running, their ninety-third defeat banked with a fortnight yet to endure. The matinee follows at 12:10, Hughes opposing Jobe.

ABRAMS STEALS THIRD IN THE TENTH AND THE MISPLAY DOES THE REST — A SECOND STRAIGHT FOR THE CAPITAL NINE, WON AT THE LAST STEP: CAPITAL NINE 6, SERAPHS 5, IN TEN INNINGS

The record-book afternoon of the columns above wanted only a proper ending, and got one. Level at five after nine, Washington put CJ Abrams aboard in the tenth, watched him steal third with the green light his manager had quietly granted — "that's what great players do," Butera ruled — and brought him home moments later when Ford's bounder to short was mishandled by Neto, the winning run scoring on the error. It closed an afternoon of honest back-and-forth: Abrams had doubled home a run, Young singled home another upon a challenge overturned, and Ortiz's single cashed two, while the ancient Trout scored on Meckler's double and Grissom's two-run homer, his eleventh, gave the visitors their innings of hope; Guzman and Ballesteros added the Seraphs' late pair, and Sinclair took the decision. Two straight now for the Capital nine after the seven-game famine these pages mourned all week — and both principals of the thirty-and-twenty brotherhood in the middle of everything, which is where the record book found them. The set concludes at 1:35 this afternoon.

The Sunday tables, then. In the American: clinched Tampa Bay holds the East by four over New York, Boston eight and a half astern; the White Sox keep the Central by a game and a half over Cleveland, the magic figure twelve, with the two principals meeting in Cleveland tomorrow evening — the fixture of the week, by this desk's lights; Houston's hold on the West is pared to two over Texas. The wild-card row: New York by four and a half over Boston, Boston six clear of the field, and the last chair Cleveland's by a single game over Toronto, with Texas two further back and Baltimore three. In the National: Atlanta by six over Philadelphia with its figure at seven; clinched Milwaukee by ten over Chicago; Los Angeles by ten over San Diego, the flag number five. The wild-card ledger: the Cubs and Quakers hold the first two chairs, the last seat San Diego's by a game and a half over Arizona, Pittsburgh six and a half back. Today's bill is the full board of fifteen, verified against the schedule, and the desk commends five engagements to the reader's lamp: at 1:35 the Subway rubber game in the Bronx, Scott opposing Schlittler and his league-leading 2.01; at 1:35 Philadelphia tries to escape Atlanta with a single scalp, Painter against Holmes; at 1:37 Cease, at 2.40, takes the hill for chair-hungry Toronto; at 2:10 Burns, fifteen-and-three, carries Cincinnati's pride into Milwaukee; and at 4:10 the desert rubber match, Quantrill against Rodriguez. The almanac reminds the reader that Tuesday the fifteenth is Roberto Clemente Day across the leagues; fourteen mornings remain to the season's final page on the seven-and-twentieth, and the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: THE FIRST TICKET TO OCTOBER IS PUNCHED BY A SINGLE SWING — CAMINERO'S FORTIETH HOME RUN, STRUCK WALK-OFF WITH THE BERTH ITSELF ABOARD: RAYS 3, ASTROS 1
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 66 · Saturday, the Twelfth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE FIRST TICKET TO OCTOBER IS PUNCHED BY A SINGLE SWING — CAMINERO'S FORTIETH HOME RUN, STRUCK WALK-OFF WITH THE BERTH ITSELF ABOARD: RAYS 3, ASTROS 1

The clinching arithmetic this paper has recited for three mornings is retired by the first pitch of the last at-bat — the Trop chants of Most Valuable Players, the manager starts hugging before the ball lands, and a club picked by the spring's wise men to finish last in its own East becomes the first in either league admitted to the postseason

The Herald has carried Tampa Bay's clinching arithmetic on its ledger all week — a magic number of two on Thursday, of one by yesterday's press — and last night the whole column of figures was retired by one swing. The account stood level at a run apiece in the ninth when the reliever Abreu offered Junior Caminero a first-pitch fastball at six-and-ninety miles to the hour; it left the bat at one hundred seven, bound for the seats beyond left-center at Tropicana Field, and the young man leaned back to admire it while his teammates were already pouring over the rail. A two-run, walk-off home run — his fortieth of the season, the first walk-off blow of his major-league life — and the Rays were in the postseason before the ball had been retrieved. "I knew it was gone," deposed the manager Cash, "so I just started watching and hugging everybody else." The batsman's own first reflection, offered through his interpreter with a smile: "It went really, really far."

The Elias bureau was kept up late certifying the occasion. Caminero is the eleventh man in the game's history to strike a walk-off homer on the day his club clinched a postseason place — a register that opens with Bobby Thomson's shot of 1951 and was last signed by Cal Raleigh in 2022, with Evan Longoria's famous midnight blow of 2011, struck in this very building, among the entries between. At three-and-twenty years and eight-and-sixty days, he is the second-youngest ever to post two seasons of forty home runs, trailing only Eddie Mathews; no Ray before him had even one such pair, the franchise's whole account of forty-homer summers now reading Peña's six-and-forty in 2007, Caminero's five-and-forty last year, and this. The crowd chanted its three initials at him, and the man seized the microphone on his way off the grass: "Tampa! This is for you!" "I thought that was the moment right there where I could really, really elevate myself to be a superstar in this game," he allowed afterward.

The evening around the thunderclap was spare and taut: Houston scratched a run across in the fourth on Diaz's force-out, Victor Mesa Jr. answered with his thirteenth homer in the fifth, and the clubs traded zeroes until the ninth, Tampa Bay managing but four hits all night and needing no more. The reliever Baker took the decision. So a club widely consigned to the cellar of its division after two barren years — its president Neander had delivered a rare preseason address insisting otherwise — becomes the first admitted to October, its tenth postseason in franchise history and first since 2023, and celebrated at last with champagne. The tables this morning: eight-and-eighty wins against nine-and-fifty defeats, the East held by three over surging New York with fifteen to play, and the beaten Astros — whose consolation is that Texas lost larger, as the card below tells — still keep the West's chair by three. The same two clubs go again at the Trop this evening, with a batting-title curiosity attached that the columns below examine at length.

News Around the League

THE MILESTONE DESK: THE STRANGEST BATTING RACE EVER RUN — THE SLUGGER ALVAREZ AT .310, THE BUNTING SPRINTER SIMPSON AT .306, AND BOTH MEN UNDER ONE ROOF ALL WEEKEND

The wires pose a question this desk cannot resist: has the game ever staged a batting-title argument between two such opposite species of hitter? Yordan Alvarez of Houston, the American's leading average at .310, is the very portrait of the modern basher — eight-and-thirty home runs, the most barreled baseballs in either league by the measuring machines' count, and an expected on-base figure the instruments rank first among all men. Chandler Simpson of Tampa Bay, at .306 and four points astern, has never hit a major-league home run in nine hundred seven-and-thirty at-bats, swings the bat slower than every qualified hitter save two, and is the only regular in the game without a single barrel to his name. No batting champion in either league's history has ever finished a season with an on-base-plus-slugging figure below .700; Simpson's stands at .691.

The sprinter's case rests on the oldest arithmetic there is: put the ball on the ground and outrun it. Eight-and-eighty percent of his hits are singles, seven-and-thirty of them never left the infield, and fourteen of those were bunts laid down like calling cards. The slugger's case rests on the newest: the machines reckon that an average runner making Simpson's contact would bat nowhere near .306, while Alvarez's figure is honestly earned off the barrel. The delicious circumstance is that the two race under one roof through Sunday, Houston being encamped at Tropicana Field — and the Herald notes besides that Alvarez sits but two home runs and a single run driven behind the league's leaders in the other two columns of the Triple Crown, a pursuit the wires have not failed to notice. This desk declines to pick a winner and merely thanks the fates for the entertainment.

THE PRODIGY DESK: DE PAULA ARRIVES PRECISELY AS PROMISED — A WALK, SOME HARD CONTACT, AND A FATHER'S TEARS AT THE RAIL IN MIAMI

The début these columns forecast on Thursday came off on schedule. Josue De Paula, one-and-twenty years of age and the sixth-ranked prospect in all the game, took his first major-league at-bats for the champions in Miami last evening as their designated hitter, and the line will be kept for sentiment rather than splendor: a fly to right, a walk honestly drawn, a caught-stealing that closed the fourth inning by way of the strike-'em-out, throw-'em-out double play, a strikeout, and a hard ground ball the first baseman did well to smother. "We saw a good walk, some hard contact, and hung in there against the lefty," ruled the manager Roberts, satisfied. "He'll get his first one soon enough."

The manner of his coming remains the marvel. Summoned directly from Double-A Tulsa — where he battered the circuit at a .303 average with a .401 on-base figure, seven-and-twenty homers, and one hundred four runs driven — he is the first Los Angeles position player in a dozen years to leap that rung entirely. "I was in disbelief," the young man confessed of the summons. "I was like, 'What, going up where?'" Before batting practice his father, up from New York for the occasion, embraced him at the rail while the boy wept. "It's a moment that you can't even describe," the elder De Paula said. "You have to live it to understand it." The club that surrounds him, it will surprise no reader, won again regardless — the full accounting stands in the card below.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: LUZARDO'S SHOULDER STIFFENS ON THE PENNANT'S HEAVIEST WEEKEND, AND ATLANTA'S THOMAS GOES TO THE INVALID LIST

The ward's gravest new entry wears Philadelphia red at the worst conceivable hour. Jesús Luzardo — second in the National in strikeouts, author only Monday of a two-hit shutout of these very Braves, the first blanking of his career — has been scratched from this evening's start in Atlanta with stiffness in the left shoulder. "We feel like it's safer to be careful with him. We don't want this to linger," explained the interim manager Mattingly, who will send an opener to the hill tonight and voices hope that his left-hander misses but a single turn. "If it lingers, it obviously would be a big blow," he allowed, "and I would be more concerned to this point. I don't feel that same way." The club, five games adrift in the East after last night's eleven-inning heartbreak, can afford neither the man's absence nor much more of September.

Across the same diamond, Atlanta placed the outfielder Lane Thomas on the invalid list yesterday morning and summoned DaShawn Keirsey Jr. from Gwinnett in his stead — a footnote at breakfast that had become a headline by midnight, for it was Keirsey's borrowed legs that scored the tying run from first base in the ninth, as the card below sings. The ward wishes Thomas and Luzardo swift mending both; the candle stays lit.

THE PITCHING DESK: NINE PITCHES, THREE STRIKEOUTS — MARTINEZ THROWS THE SEASON'S FOURTH IMMACULATE INNING, TWO OF THEM NOW IN SERPENT LIVERY

The connoisseur's item of the evening was thrown in the sixth inning in Phoenix. Justin Martinez, the Arizona right-hander lately returned from his second visit to the elbow surgeons, faced three Texas batsmen and dismissed them on nine pitches entire — Langford struck out, Carter struck out swinging at a fastball registered at one hundred two and a half miles to the hour, and Burger struck out on three straight swings, the middle offering a tick faster still. The scorers call it an immaculate inning; the season has now produced four of them in the major leagues, and remarkably two belong to Arizona, Soroka having turned the trick back on the thirtieth of March. It is the fifth in the franchise's annals.

The larger figure is the quiet one beneath: since returning from an absence of four months and more, Martinez has worked seven and two-thirds innings without surrendering an earned run. A bullpen that gets such an arm back in September has found money in an old coat, and the desert nine's October pretensions — advanced at length in the card below — are the stronger for it.

THE ALMANAC DESK: THREE GRAND SLAMS FLY IN A SINGLE EVENING, AND THE WEEK'S LEDGER OF LOADED-BASES THUNDER SWELLS TO FIVE

The scorers were kept busy at the grandest denomination the game prints. Three times last night a man came to the plate with the bases full and emptied them at a stroke: Garrett Mitchell in Milwaukee, whose blast crowned an eight-run fifth and stands as the Brewers' first slam of the season; Kyle Tucker in Miami, whose seventh-inning drive turned a taut affair into a procession; and Rafael Devers in San Francisco, whose fifth-inning answer hauled his club within two, though the evening was lost regardless — the only one of the three struck in a defeat.

The Herald's readers will note the week's larger pattern, for these pages recorded George Lombard Jr.'s slam at the Stadium on Wednesday night and Anthony Volpe's on Thursday: five grand slams inside three evenings, two of them the first and second of the Yankees' season, one the first of Milwaukee's. The desk offers no theory beyond September itself — the month when pitchers tire, rosters swell, and the bases seem always to be occupied — and moves along before the gods of small samples take offense.

The Rest of the Card

THE SECOND TICKET OF THE NIGHT IS PUNCHED WITH TWENTY RUNS TO SPARE — TWO PITCHERS, TWO HITS ALLOWED, AND EVERY MAN IN THE ORDER SAFELY ABOARD: SUDS MEN 20, QUEEN CITY NINE 0

An hour or so after Tampa Bay's celebration began, Milwaukee staged its own, and left an exclamation point where other clubs leave a scorecard. The Brewers clinched their eighth postseason berth in nine seasons by the widest margin any club has ever enjoyed on a clinching day — the Elias bureau certifies the twenty-run cushion surpasses seventeen-run affairs by the 2001 Braves and 1996 Yankees — and did it with an economy that borders on insolence: Dustin May gave six innings of two hits, the reliever Stallings carried the last three without permitting a safety at all, and every member of the starting nine recorded a hit among the three-and-twenty. Eight runs crossed inside two innings; eight more piled into the fifth, crowned by Garrett Mitchell's grand slam, the club's first of the year, of which the almanac desk above has more; Brice Turang drove in four to reach ninety on the season, and William Contreras drove in six. Even the defense showed off — the rookie Luis Lara, whose walk-off knock these pages sang on Wednesday, went above the right-center fence to rob Suárez so cleanly that the umpires, seeing the ball vanish, signaled a home run until the young man produced it from his glove. "Air Lara," his center fielder shrugged.

The house took its champagne in moderation: a clubhouse toast, no showers, the manager Murphy spending his remarks on clubhouse men, bullpen catchers, and cooks. "You have to celebrate the moments, no matter how big or how small," said Mitchell, before appending the September qualifier: "We still got a lot more to go." The arithmetic behind the restraint: two-and-ninety wins, a franchise-record six-and-thirty games above the waterline, the Central held by ten over Chicago, and the best record in either league — with the flag itself still formally unclinched. The clubs meet again this evening; the beaten Reds, twice-hit and four times beaten running, may be forgiven for consulting the schedule's fine print.

ON THE CITY'S NIGHT OF REMEMBRANCE, THE FIREFIGHTER'S SON STRIKES THE TELLING BLOW — BELLINGER'S THREE-RUN DRIVE CARRIES THE SUBWAY OPENER: YANKEES 6, METROPOLITANS 4

The evening this paper promised would carry more than baseball kept its word. Boone, Judge, and Cole bore a memorial wreath into Monument Park in the afternoon; the ceremonial first pitch was thrown by Brielle Saracini, whose father captained the second of the stolen airliners, and was caught — by no accident of assignment — by Cody Bellinger, whose own father Clay wore the pinstripes in 2001 and afterward took up the firefighter's helmet in Arizona. In the second inning the son hit a three-run homer off the rookie McLean, Anthony Volpe — yesterday's hero — crossing ahead of him. "Today was a day where it felt bigger than the game, bigger than yourself," Bellinger said. Ben Rice added his seven-and-thirtieth homer, the club's leading count, swinging a bat stamped with the fire department's crest; the chants of U-S-A began with the anthem and never quite subsided.

The game beneath the occasion was honest work. Carlos Rodón, calling the assignment "heavy" and pitching like a man unburdened, gave six and a third innings of two runs, one earned, with eight strikeouts — his longest outing of the season; Headrick speared Lindor's two-out liner with the bases loaded in the seventh; and Bednar earned a five-out save the hard way, escaping a loaded-bases jam in the eighth for the price of a sacrifice fly and absorbing Ewing's ninth-inning homer before Soto banged into the double play that ended it. New York's fourth consecutive victory holds the East's gap at three behind clinched Tampa Bay and stretches the first wild-card chair's cushion to five and a half over Boston, whose own stumble is entered below. The clubs resume at 1:35 this afternoon, Cole taking the ball.

BEHIND AFTER THE NINTH, THE TENTH, AND THE ELEVENTH BEGAN, AND WINNERS ALL THE SAME — KIM TIES IT, BALDWIN ENDS IT, AND THE EAST'S GAP GROWS TO FIVE: BRAVES 6, BROTHERLY LOVE NINE 5, IN ELEVEN INNINGS

The set this paper billed as a possible settling of the National's East opened with a game that may stand as the season's maddest inside nine hundred miles of the Miami carnival. Philadelphia led by a run entering the home ninth and by a run again in both the tenth and the eleventh, and lost anyway — Atlanta rallying in all three innings, the last word belonging to Drake Baldwin, whose double scored Ha-Seong Kim from first base, headfirst across the plate, moments after Kim's own two-out single had leveled the account. The manager Weiss emptied his bench of twelve position players, and three of the four runs Atlanta scored from the ninth inning onward were tallied by borrowed legs: DaShawn Keirsey Jr., promoted only that morning as the ward above records, tore home from first on Murphy's ninth-inning single when the ball was bobbled in center; Brewer Hicklen, sent in for Olson, beat the throw on Dubón's sacrifice fly in the tenth. "People got their money's worth tonight," ruled Olson, whose eight-and-thirtieth homer had opened the scoring in the first inning, several lifetimes earlier.

Sale's seven innings of three hits, Riley's seventeenth homer, and a bullpen that permitted no earned run across four frames underwrote the theatrics; Philadelphia's Hill drove in three with a second-inning double and then, cruelly, supplied the ninth-inning bobble. For Kim, written off at a .068 average in the spring and exiled to Gwinnett by July, it is a second enormous hit in three weeks, and the wires note his tying knock left the bat at one hundred six miles to the hour. The consequence is stern arithmetic: Atlanta's lead over the second-place visitors stands at five with a dozen games to play after Sunday, and Philadelphia — Luzardo scratched, as the ward reports, an opener to face Mahle tonight — must now sweep what remains of the set merely to leave town closer than it arrived.

THE ALLEGHENY PARADE HALTS AT CLARK AND ADDISON — BREGMAN COLLECTS THREE HITS AND HIS FIVE-AND-TWENTIETH, AND THE NORTH SIDERS' OWN SLIDE ENDS AT FOUR: NORTH SIDERS 12, ALLEGHENYS 2

Two streaks walked into Wrigley Field and both were shot. Pittsburgh's four-game winning parade, saluted in yesterday's columns, was dismantled by the second inning; Chicago's four-game losing skid, mourned in the same pages, ended in a sixteen-hit exhibition. Alex Bregman did the heaviest lifting with three hits, his five-and-twentieth homer, and two runs driven; Michael Busch drove in three, Seiya Suzuki collected three hits with a triple among them, and Shota Imanaga carried six innings for his tenth victory. Cruz's first-inning single and Reynolds's seventeenth homer were the visitors' whole reply. The desk notes for the faithful that Crow-Armstrong singled home his eight-and-ninetieth run but left the theft column unmoved at six-and-thirty — the forty-forty ledger still wants four steals, and the calendar now offers but fourteen games. The clubs go again at 2:20 this afternoon, and the bill is the day's pearl: Skenes against Holmes.

MEIDROTH HOMERS TWICE AND IT AVAILS NOTHING — A FOURTH STRAIGHT DEFEAT SHAVES THE CENTRAL'S CHAIR TO HALF A GAME: MOUND CITY NINE 7, WHITE SOX 3

Chicago's evening produced a curiosity and a crisis. The curiosity: Chase Meidroth supplied both early runs with a pair of solo homers, his thirteenth and fourteenth. The crisis: everything else. St. Louis answered patiently and then decisively — a three-run fifth built on Burleson's run-scoring single, Báez's second double of the night, and Bernal's single, with Bernal adding another run home in the seventh — while Graceffo, now the owner of an eight-and-one record, held the visitors quiet through a rain-delayed evening. Burleson's two runs driven lift his season's count to one hundred six, second in the National. The White Sox have now dropped four running, and the arithmetic turns grave: Cleveland's victory, entered below, trims the Central's chair to half a game — the thinnest it has been all September. The Cardinals, for their part, play the spoiler's part with evident relish; the clubs go again at 7:15 tonight.

TWO IN THE SEVENTH, THREE IN THE NINTH, AND THE SUMMIT WITHIN HALF A GAME — ROCCHIO'S DOUBLE SEALS THE LAKE ERIE PURSUIT: LAKE ERIE MEN 5, NORTH STARS 2

Cleveland's chase of the Central's chair, conducted these three weeks with a bailiff's patience, drew within half a game of the wobbling White Sox. Angel Martínez supplied the lead with a two-run homer in the seventh, Bazzana crossing ahead of him; Minnesota drew level within the half-inning; and the ninth settled it — the go-ahead run scampering home on a wild pitch, by the wires' account with Bazzana again the runner, before Brayan Rocchio doubled two more across for the cushion. Smith closed his six-and-thirtieth save behind Gaddis's decision, and the Lake Erie men hold besides the American's last wild-card chair, two clear of Toronto with the tiebreaker long since banked, as this paper has recited to the point of song. The clubs resume in Minnesota at 4:10 this afternoon.

BEAVERS OPENS THE EVENING WITH THUNDER AND FIVE MORE CROSS BEFORE SCHERZER ESCAPES THE SECOND — AND THE ROOKIE TRIO STANDS LEVEL AT ONE-AND-THIRTY: BIRDS 7, TORONTOS 4

Baltimore's evening was decided almost before Toronto batted. Dylan Beavers opened the game with a home run, and the second inning fell in like a poorly built wall: five runs, Kjerstad and Cowser driving in three between them before Beavers returned to single home two more — three runs driven for the leadoff man in all. Chris Bassitt made the early fortune stand across a workmanlike evening while the ancient Scherzer, now two-and-eight, absorbed the damage; Mayo's three-and-twentieth homer supplied the seventh run, and Garcia closed the door after Bateman's two-run homer, his first of the year, made the ninth briefly interesting. The Birds have won two running and stand three from the last chair — obstinate guests at a party they were not invited to.

Toronto's consolation was historic all the same: Kazuma Okamoto struck his one-and-thirtieth homer, and the freshman company this paper convened on Wednesday now stands level — Okamoto, Murakami, and Stewart, one-and-thirty apiece, the only thirty-homer rookie trio the game has ever produced, climbing in lockstep. The Torontos themselves have dropped two running and sit two behind Cleveland's chair; they host the Birds again at 3:07 this afternoon.

THE EIGHTEENTH VICTORY MUST WAIT — KANSAS CITY STRIKES THRICE EARLY, AND THE LEAGUE'S WINNINGEST ARM IS BEATEN AT FENWAY: ROYALS 3, CRIMSON HOSE 2

The errand this paper flagged in yesterday's bill — Gray in pursuit of an eighteenth victory — ended in the ledger's other column. Kansas City reached the great man for single runs in the first and a pair in the third, Carter Jensen doubling twice and scoring twice while Perez, Jensen himself, and Pasquantino cashed a run apiece, and the visitors then defended the small fortune for six innings: Lugo took the decision, and Cruz recorded the final outs for his seventh save. Boston's reply was Gasper's ninth homer and Abreu's run-scoring double, and no more; the Crimson Hose have now dropped three running, though the second wild-card chair remains theirs by five clear games. Gray departs at seventeen-and-five with his figure at 2.76 and his next chance ahead; the Royals, playing out September with the young Jensen — one-and-thirty doubles now beside his three-and-twenty homers — providing the education, have quietly won two straight. The matinee follows at 1:35.

TUCKER EMPTIES THE BASES AND THE CHAMPIONS COUNT TO NINETY — AN EIGHTH STRAIGHT VICTORY ON THE NIGHT OF THE PRODIGY'S DÉBUT: DODGERS 6, FISH 2

Los Angeles made its ninetieth victory of the season look like an errand run before supper. Kyle Tucker supplied five of the six runs himself — a sacrifice fly in the third, then a seventh-inning grand slam, the almanac desk's third exhibit above, with a triple banked besides in a three-hit evening — while Blake Snell struck out eight across five and two-thirds innings of one run, his figure now a gaudy 1.91. Miami's ten hits of scattered singles-and-doubles industry produced only Ramírez's double and Caissie's sacrifice fly, and the champions' eighth consecutive victory — a season's best, stretching the run begun before this paper's week of chronicling their surge — leaves the West's flag number at five. The rookie De Paula's first evening, attended by his weeping father and sung at length in the columns above, came attached to the winning side, as first evenings in that livery generally do. The clubs meet again at 4:10, Glasnow and his unbeaten four-and-nought taking the hill.

SEVEN RUNS INSIDE THREE INNINGS, THEN A LONG AFTERNOON OF HOLDING THE DOOR — DEVERS' GRAND SLAM FALLS TWO SHORT, AND THE FIFTH STRAIGHT IS BANKED: FRIARS 7, BAY NINE 5

San Diego played its scoring like a man spending his whole purse before noon: two runs in the second, five in the third, and not another all evening. Freddy Fermin doubled twice among two runs driven, Bogaerts cashed two with a double of his own, and the unheralded Dustin Harris singled home one run and tripled home another. Then came the holding action — Rafael Devers' fifth-inning grand slam, celebrated dutifully in the almanac columns above, hauled the hosts from seven-to-one to seven-to-five — and the visitors' bullpen simply refused further correspondence, Miller sealing his five-and-thirtieth save. Ray took the decision. The Friars have now won five running, their brightest run of the summer's late innings, and hold the National's last chair by half a game over Arizona, whose own demolition work is entered below — the two clubs fated, as this paper has noted, to conclude the season against one another. The set resumes at 4:05 this afternoon.

CARROLL RETURNS FROM THE EXAMINERS SWINGING, MARTE DOUBLES TWICE, AND NINE RUNS FALL ON TEXAS IN TWO INNINGS: SONORAN NINE 9, RANGERS 1

The back that sent Corbin Carroll to the imaging machines on Tuesday, as the ward then reported, appears to have been given a clean bill: the outfielder struck his twentieth homer among two runs driven as Arizona buried Texas beneath a four-run fifth and a five-run sixth. Ketel Marte doubled twice and drove in three, Moreno singled home two, and Arenado added his four-and-twentieth homer to the pile; Pederson's run-scoring double accounted for the visitors' whole scoring. The connoisseurs' portion of the evening — Martinez's nine-pitch, three-strikeout sixth — is served at proper length in the pitching columns above. The consequences cut both ways along the wild-card row: the Sonoran nine keep their deficit for the last chair at half a game behind San Diego, while Texas, thrice beaten running, drifts three behind Houston in the West and three from the row's last seat — a September chase leaking oil at every joint. The clubs go again at 8:10 this evening, Rocker opposing Pfaadt.

RODRÍGUEZ WINS THE TENTH INNING'S FIRST HALF AND WALTON THE SECOND — THE WHITE ELEPHANTS WALK OFF BEFORE THE SMALLEST HOUSE IN THE LEAGUE: WHITE ELEPHANTS 6, MARINERS 5, IN TEN INNINGS

The evening in West Sacramento was decided twice in five minutes. Julio Rodríguez singled home the go-ahead run in the top of the tenth, and Donovan Walton answered in the bottom with a two-run, walk-off homer — his seventh — before a gathering of 8,682 that made up in noise what it wanted in number. The middle innings belonged to the young: Lawrence Butler's two-run homer built the early lead, and Seattle's answer came from Lazaro Montes, the one-and-twenty-year-old colossus whose four-hundred-seventy-four-foot thunderclap these pages measured on Wednesday, whose third career homer — a two-run blow that leveled the account at four — suggests the large type this desk predicted is being set already. Roycroft took the decision. The Athletics have won two running and seven of ten — the September mischief-maker's badge, worn this year in green and gold — while the Mariners' long season leaks another game. The same clubs close the league's evening at 9:40 tonight.

A FOUR-RUN SIXTH SETTLES THE MATTER IN DETROIT — GREENE TRIPLES AND DOUBLES, DINGLER STRIKES HIS SEVEN-AND-TWENTIETH, AND THE ROX DROP A FIFTH STRAIGHT: MOTOR CITY NINE 6, ROX 2

Colorado scratched ahead on an unearned run in the fifth, and Detroit answered with the game entire: Max Clark leveled it with a homer in the home half, and the sixth produced four more — Riley Greene's run-scoring triple, Dillon Dingler's two-run homer, his seven-and-twentieth with his seven-and-eightieth run driven besides, a count that keeps the young catcher among the American's leading five, and Clark scampering home on a wild pitch. Greene added a run-scoring double in the eighth for good measure — a triple and a double on the evening for the left fielder. Valdez carried six innings for the decision and Jansen sealed his nineteenth save; Veen's ninth-inning single spared the visitors a quieter line. The Motor City nine have won two running and continue the autumn schooling of their young men; the Rox, five times beaten in succession and seven-and-thirty games adrift, are running out of September to lose. The matinee follows at 1:10.

SEVEN DEFEATS, AND ENOUGH — A THREE-RUN EIGHTH ENDS THE CAPITAL FAMINE, WITH VIVAS SUPPLYING THE DECIDING FREIGHT: NATS 4, ANAHEIM NINE 3

Washington's seven-game losing spell, chronicled in these pages with mounting sympathy, was broken at last by an eighth inning of honest work. Trailing by a run — the ancient Trout had opened the evening with his one-and-twentieth homer, and Moore's single had restored the visitors' lead in the seventh — the Nationals stacked three: Pinckney's sacrifice fly leveled it, and Jorbit Vivas doubled two more across for the lead. Moore's ninth-inning double made the margin nervous before Tolman closed his second save; Beeter took the decision. James Wood, whose single had cashed the club's first run, banked his five-and-seventieth run driven in the bargain. The Anaheim nine, one-and-ninety times beaten, played their betters hard once more and lost once more — the spoiler's trade conducted without the spoils. The clubs resume at 4:05 this afternoon.

The Saturday tables carry two flags of certification. In the American: Tampa Bay — clinched, as the columns above rejoice — holds the East by three over New York, Boston eight and a half astern; the White Sox cling to the Central by half a game over Cleveland, the thinnest edge of their September; Houston keeps the West by three over Texas. The wild-card row: New York and Boston seated in comfort, the last chair Cleveland's by two over Toronto, with Texas and Baltimore three back. In the National: Atlanta by five over Philadelphia with the principals at it again tonight; Milwaukee — clinched, and by twenty runs — leads Chicago by ten; Los Angeles by eleven over San Diego, the West's flag number at five. The wild-card ledger: the Cubs and Philadelphia share the first two chairs at two and a half clear, the last seat San Diego's by half a game over Arizona, Pittsburgh five and a half back, St. Louis six and a half. Today's bill is the full board of fifteen, all verified against the schedule, and the desk commends six engagements to the reader's lamp: at 1:35 the Subway matter resumes in the Bronx, Thornton opposing Cole; at 2:20 the pearl of the day at Wrigley, Skenes against Holmes; at 4:10 the champions send the unbeaten Glasnow against Miami with their flag number at five; at 6:10 the clinched Rays host Houston, Lambert opposing Seymour, with the batting-title curiosity of the columns above sharing the premises; at 7:15 Philadelphia, its ace scratched and an opener summoned, faces Mahle in Atlanta wanting urgent amends; and at 8:10 Texas seeks its footing in the desert against Pfaadt. The almanac notes Roberto Clemente Day upon the fifteenth; fifteen mornings remain to the season's final page on the seven-and-twentieth, and the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: ONE DAY BACK FROM EXILE, VOLPE STRIKES A GRAND SLAM, DRIVES IN FIVE, AND TAKES A CURTAIN CALL — THE CLUB THAT WAITED A SEASON FOR A SLAM HAS NOW STRUCK TWO IN AS MANY NIGHTS: YANKEES 10, COLORADANS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 65 · Friday, the Eleventh of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 5 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

ONE DAY BACK FROM EXILE, VOLPE STRIKES A GRAND SLAM, DRIVES IN FIVE, AND TAKES A CURTAIN CALL — THE CLUB THAT WAITED A SEASON FOR A SLAM HAS NOW STRUCK TWO IN AS MANY NIGHTS: YANKEES 10, COLORADANS 3

The shortstop of yesteryear returns as a second baseman and collects three hits, García Jr. reaches thirty homers with number one-and-ninety driven besides, and a six-run seventh buries Colorado — all while Fried's evening ends after but ten outs and the relief corps quietly banks the victory

When August was young, New York sent Anthony Volpe away to the minors, and no man could say with certainty when — or whether — he would return. The wires tell it plainly: nothing was promised him. He went down, learned a new post at second base across nineteen minor-league starts, hit until one clubhouse wit swore he "became Barry Bonds all of a sudden," and waited. On Wednesday, as this paper reported in yesterday's ward, Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s sprained thumb opened the door. On Thursday evening Volpe walked through it swinging.

The accounting: three hits in four visits, five runs driven, and — with the bases loaded in a six-run seventh — a grand slam off the reliever Herget, driven to right field, his third such blow as a professional and his first since the World Series of 2024. The Stadium, which had waited the entire season for a grand slam until young Lombard supplied one Wednesday night, has now witnessed two in as many evenings — and last night the author of the first stood at shortstop while the author of the second manned second base beside him, the first appearance of Volpe's major-league life at that station. The crowd of forty thousand called him back out of the dugout for a bow. "There was nothing guaranteed," the returned man said afterward. "I wanted to be ready and prepared." His manager Boone put it simpler: "He had a massive impact tonight, and it's really good to see him."

The rest of the evening's freight: Luis García Jr. opened the scoring with a two-run blast in the first — his thirtieth of the year, his ninetieth and one-and-ninetieth runs driven — and Bellinger added two doubles and a sacrifice fly. The asterisk on the box belongs to Max Fried, whose evening ended after but ten outs; seven strikeouts in three and a third, yet the fastness left him, and Schreiber's inning and a third of relief took the decision. Colorado's answers — Karros's eleventh homer, McCarthy's triple — were footnotes by the seventh. New York has won three running, stands a season's-best two-and-twenty games above the waterline at four-and-eighty wins, and — with Tampa Bay beaten in Atlanta, as the card below relates — draws within three of the East's chair. The Bronx hosts the Mets this evening on a night of solemn remembrance, of which the columns below have much to say.

News Around the League

A QUARTER-CENTURY SINCE THE TOWERS FELL: THE GAME PAUSES THIS DAY TO REMEMBER, WITH THE SUBWAY MEETING IN THE BRONX AT THE CENTER OF THE OBSERVANCE

The Herald sets aside its usual ornament for this item, for the date at the top of this page is the eleventh of September, and five-and-twenty years have now passed since the morning of 2001. The league marks the anniversary across every park tonight: a moment of silence before each contest, dedicated lineup cards and base jewels, "God Bless America" at the seventh-inning stretch, and upon every head — player, manager, coach, and umpire alike — a cap bearing the patch We Shall Never Forget. In Toronto the Blue Jays' caps will carry the Canadian and American flags together.

The center of the observance sits, as it must, in New York, where Mets and Yankees meet this evening at the Stadium wearing caps honoring the first responders — the firemen, police, and rescue workers of that morning. Across town at Citi Field, the league and the Mets convene a meal-packing effort for families in need, led by men who wore the orange and blue in that wounded autumn: Mike Piazza, whose September homer lifted a grieving city, with David Wright and Al Leiter beside him. The league's network has besides premiered a two-hour chronicle, When America Took the Field, on baseball's small part in the healing. This paper, which trades daily in mock heroics, knows the genuine article when it sees it, and lowers its voice accordingly.

THE MILESTONE DESK: SEVEN-AND-FORTY HOME RUNS FOR THE MINOR-LEAGUER FISCHER — NO MAN HAS HIT SO MANY IN A BUSH-LEAGUE SUMMER THIS CENTURY

The minors have produced their thunderclap of the season. Andrew Fischer, two-and-twenty years of age, a first-round selection of Milwaukee only last summer and now the fifth-ranked prospect in that organization's books, struck his seven-and-fortieth home run of the campaign — the most any minor-leaguer has amassed in a single season this century. The wires place the figure fifth in the modern ledger kept since 1963, trailing only Bill McNulty's five-and-fifty, Gorman Thomas's one-and-fifty, Ron Kittle's fifty, and Tony Solaita's nine-and-forty — company of the rarest sort.

The arithmetic of the young New Jerseyan's summer beggars belief: twenty homers in four-and-fifty games at High-A Wisconsin, a promotion at June's end, and seven-and-twenty more in nine-and-sixty games at Double-A Biloxi, with a .272 average, a .411 on-base figure, a .656 slugging mark, and one hundred thirteen runs driven across the whole. The Herald notes that the parent club in Milwaukee already owns the National's best record and its likeliest Cy Young laureate, of whom the pitching desk below has more; the barons of the Cream City appear to be stockpiling thunder against winters yet to come.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: PITTSBURGH'S ALL-STAR ASHCRAFT GOES TO THE INVALID LIST AT THE WORST POSSIBLE HOUR, AND THE WARD'S SMALLER LEDGER BESIDES

The ward's gravest new admission wears Pittsburgh gray. Braxton Ashcraft, an All-Star this summer and the owner of a 3.65 figure across one hundred sixty-five and a third innings with one hundred seventy-three strikeouts, has been placed upon the fifteen-day invalid list with discomfort in the right arm, the sentence written backward to the seventh of September. The first testing, his manager Don Kelly reports, "does not appear to be anything structural" — the ward exhales — but the calendar is unkind: the earliest lawful return falls on the two-and-twentieth, the season's final week, and the wires call even that unlikely. The right-hander Antwone Kelly is summoned from Indianapolis to fill the post, and the timing sharpens the value of what Jones supplied last evening, as the card below sings.

The smaller ledger: Washington's Nasim Nuñez, whose six-and-forty stolen bases lead the National, has gone to the bereavement list, and the Herald extends the Capital nine's speedster its unfeigned sympathies. Minnesota welcomes Austin Martin back from the ten-day list. And the mending wing reports steady traffic — Shea Langeliers taking rehabilitation at Las Vegas for the Athletics, Kansas City's Maikel Garcia and Connor Seabold at Omaha, Colorado's Sean Sullivan at Albuquerque, and Houston's Brice Matthews at Sugar Land. Swift returns to all; the candle stays lit.

THE PITCHING DESK: CAN ANY MAN CATCH THE MIZ? — MILWAUKEE'S FLAMETHROWER LEADS THE NATIONAL IN NEARLY EVERYTHING AS THE CY YOUNG QUESTION ENTERS ITS FINAL WEEKS

The wires put the question squarely this morning, and the Herald takes it up: is the National League's Cy Young argument already finished? Jacob Misiorowski of Milwaukee — four-and-twenty years old, called "The Miz" by men who have run out of superlatives — leads the league in the earned-run figure at 1.95, in strikeouts at two hundred six-and-thirty, and in the walks-and-hits reckoning at 0.80, with fourteen victories entered besides. The testimony of the measuring machines borders on the fantastic: one thousand and ten pitches thrown at one hundred miles to the hour or better this season, where no other starting pitcher of the tracking era had ever thrown more than three hundred seven-and-thirty in a summer. His June engagement against Philadelphia — fifteen strikeouts, one hit — reads like something from the age this paper affects to inhabit.

Yet the pursuit is genuine. Atlanta's ancient marvel Sale carries a 2.10 figure with fourteen victories of his own; Philadelphia offers a brace of contenders in Sánchez, whose seventeen victories lead the league, and Luzardo, second in strikeouts at two hundred one-and-twenty; and Arizona's Rodriguez has fifteen victories against a 2.55 figure. The wires' judgment, which this desk endorses: the prize is The Miz's to lose, but a stumble in the final fortnight would hand the electors an agonizing choice. He takes the ball again with the arithmetic watching — as does every man named above, for their clubs' October fortunes ride the same arms.

The Rest of the Card

PÉREZ AND MARTINEZ TRADE ZEROES DEEP INTO THE AFTERNOON, ALBIES RISES FROM A BENCH HE NEVER WANTED, AND THE CLINCHING TICKET GOES UNPUNCHED: TOMAHAWK NINE 3, TAMPA MEN 1

The Thursday finale this paper flagged for the noon lamp delivered a pitchers' argument of the old school. Martín Pérez — who strolled into the Atlanta clubhouse in hat and sunglasses and changed the music to salsa, a man at his ease — gave seven scoreless innings on four hits; Tampa Bay's Nick Martinez answered with six and a third scoreless of his own on a mere eight-and-sixty pitches, two singles the whole damage against him, and was nonetheless lifted — "we have a lot of confidence in our bullpen," he shrugged afterward, and the confidence proved misplaced. In the eighth, Ozzie Albies — informed by text the night before that he would rest, and having lobbied against the day off in vain — rose from the bench and dented the right-center wall with a pinch-hit triple off Kelly. Riley singled him home through a drawn-in infield, Yastrzemski doubled, and Ha-Seong Kim's two-run single made it three across — equal to what Atlanta had scored in its previous four-and-thirty innings combined. Mesa Jr.'s ninth-inning homer off Iglesias, his twelfth, was Tampa Bay's lone reply against the two-and-thirtieth save.

The consequences run in two directions. Atlanta halts a three-game slide, avoids the sweep, and fattens its East lead to four over Philadelphia — whom the Tomahawk nine host beginning this very evening, a set that may settle the division. Tampa Bay's clinching scenarios, laid out in yesterday's columns, went unconsummated — but Texas's defeat in Seattle trimmed the arithmetic regardless, and the wires certify the Tampa men stand a single victory from October: the berth can be sealed tonight at home against Houston. Their East lead over surging New York, meanwhile, thins to three.

THE GHOST OF NOVEMBER 2022 WALKS AT THE BANK — JAVIER CARRIES A NO-HITTER INTO THE FIFTH ON THE FIELD OF HIS MASTERPIECE, AND THE ROOKIE SMITH SETTLES IT IN THE NINTH: ASTROS 2, PHILS 1

Cristian Javier had not pitched at Citizens Bank Park since the fourth game of the 2022 World Series, when he threw six hitless innings at this same lineup's ancestors; his catcher Vázquez reminded him of it on the Tuesday bus ride, and his manager Espada joked — half joked — about a repetition. The man nearly obliged: a walk to Schwarber to open the first, then the minimum through four, no hit until the fifth, six innings of one-run ball in all. Zack Wheeler matched him grimly — seven innings, nine strikeouts, a single run — and the affair reached the ninth level at one, Trammell's early double and Stott's fielder's-choice answer the only entries. Whereupon the rookie Cam Smith turned on the All-Star closer Duran and drove the ball to center for his twentieth homer and the lead. "It felt like the playoffs," said Smith, and the crowd of seven-and-thirty thousand would not dispute him. Abreu struck out the side in the eighth for the victory; Hader sealed his five-and-twentieth save.

The standings take note twice over. Houston banks the series and keeps the American West's chair by three over Texas, whose Seattle misfortune is next door. Philadelphia, its bats gone quiet at the worst hour, has lost an untimely series at home, falls four behind Atlanta, and travels tonight to the very yard of its tormentors for three games that may decide the East — Nola against Sale, a bill worth any reader's evening.

THE HATTERS OF STETSON HOLD THEIR SEMINAR — TWELVE STRIKEOUTS FOR DEGROM, ELEVEN FOR GILBERT, AND ONE SWING FROM RODRÍGUEZ UNDOES AN EVENING OF NEAR-PERFECTION: PUGET SOUND MEN 4, ARLINGTON MEN 3

The pearl this paper flagged in yesterday's bill proved genuine. Jacob deGrom and Logan Gilbert, Florida-born alumni both of little Stetson University, met for the fourth time this season and staged the finest pitching seminar of the year: deGrom perfect through five innings, ten strikeouts before a single man reached, the first hit a comebacker off his own glove, six scoreless in all with twelve strikeouts — the most of his Texas tenure; Gilbert answering with seven innings and a season's-best eleven. Three-and-twenty strikeouts between the two starters, the most in any game since Sale and Snell in the August of 2024 — and, by the Elias bureau's certification, the first time in the game's recorded history that two starters from the same college struck out ten men apiece in the same contest. Pederson's two-run homer and Lopez's bunt single had built Texas a 3-0 lead upon deGrom's work.

Then came the seventh and the reliever Junis, who retired not a single man: a run home on Canzone's single, and then Julio Rodríguez met a line drive to left-center with two aboard — his one-and-twentieth homer, four runs across in the blink of an inning. Muñoz worked the ninth for his seven-and-twentieth save, and six innings of one-hit perfection from the game's most decorated arm dissolved into a bullpen defeat. The cost is counted in Arlington: the Arlington men fall three behind Houston in the West and two from the wild-card row's last chair, their September chase leaking games it cannot spare. The clubs go again tonight in the desert — no, the reader's pardon: Texas travels to Arizona while Seattle calls upon the Athletics, both engagements on the late bill.

FROM THE SURGEON'S COUCH TO THE SEVENTH INNING WITHOUT A HIT — JONES BLANKS THE WHITE SOX ON ONE SAFETY, AND THE SWEEP BELONGS TO PITTSBURGH: BUCCANEERS 2, WHITE SOX 0

The bill this paper set for Thursday night — Jones against Chicago's astonishing opener Smith — kept every promise. Smith supplied his two scoreless innings and departed with his figure at a scarcely credible 0.50; it was what followed that made the evening. Jared Jones, who submitted to the elbow surgeons in the May of 2025 and passed, by his own accounting, "a lot of hours on the couch watching the guys play," carried a no-hitter into the seventh inning with two out, when Colson Montgomery doubled off the right-field wall. Jones retired the next man and handed over a line of seven innings, one hit, eight strikeouts. Oneil Cruz supplied the offense entire — his eighteenth homer in the fourth, a run-scoring single in the eighth — and Pittsburgh's own Montgomery closed the ninth for his twelfth save — the Chicago Montgomery, Colson, having authored the only hit against Pittsburgh all night. Fedde absorbed the defeat.

The ledgers on both sides are eloquent. Pittsburgh has won four running and eight of its last ten, completes its first road sweep since the July of 2025, and stands above the waterline for the first time since late July — with Ashcraft's absence, mourned in the ward above, making Jones's economy of arms doubly dear. The Buccaneers proceed directly to Wrigley Field for this afternoon's engagement with the Cubs. Chicago's south-side club, meanwhile, was held to two hits, struck out eleven times, has dropped three running — and yet retains the Central's chair by a game and a half over idle Cleveland, the divisional number holding at fourteen. The Guardians open in Minnesota tonight; the arithmetic of that race now runs through both cities at once.

The Friday tables stand thus. In the American: Tampa Bay holds the East by three over New York, Boston seven and a half astern, and can seal its October berth this very night; the White Sox keep the Central by a game and a half over Cleveland; Houston keeps the West by three over Texas. The wild-card row: New York and Boston in comfort, the last chair Cleveland's by one over Toronto, Texas two back, Baltimore three. In the National: Atlanta by four over Philadelphia, with the principals meeting head-on in Atlanta beginning tonight; Milwaukee by ten over Chicago; Los Angeles by eleven over San Diego. The wild-card ledger: Philadelphia's chair three and a half clear, the Cubs two and a half, and the last seat San Diego's by half a game over Arizona, Pittsburgh four and a half back. Tonight the full board of fifteen returns, and the bill is heavy with consequence: at 2:20 the Buccaneers carry their four-game parade into Wrigley, Dotel opposing Imanaga; at 7:05 the Subway meeting of Mets and Yankees at the Stadium, McLean against Rodón, played beneath the remembrance the columns above describe; at 7:10 Tampa Bay's clinching chance against Houston, Ullola opposing Rasmussen, while in Boston the seventeen-game winner Gray seeks his eighteenth against Kansas City, and in Miami the champions arrive with the prodigy De Paula's début expected, as this paper reported yesterday; at 7:15 the summit of the National East opens in Atlanta, Nola against Sale; at 8:10 Cleveland begins its pursuit in Minnesota, Messick opposing Bradley, with Chicago at St. Louis three-quarters of an hour later. The almanac notes Roberto Clemente Day upon the fifteenth; sixteen mornings remain to the season's final page on the seven-and-twentieth, and the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~
